### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Always ask the prospect's budget first; if they resist, get a range, then offer tiered options ("option 1/2/3," e.g. 50-70k, 70-100k, 100-150k) and keep spinning back until they reveal a number (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS I Learned Working in Tech Sales")
- Budget-extraction reframe (verbatim): "My goal isn't to overcharge you. I'm trying to understand if we're the right fit — because if your budget doesn't align with our pricing, it won't work. So is there a range we can work with?" (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Anchor high, then strip services down to hit their number: "Okay, what price works for you?" → reduce scope to reach it (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Speed + guarantee can override price: "It costs this, we guarantee it's done by this date or we give your money back." (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Premium-positioning principle: never be cheapest; set a premium price tied to a pain so strong they become "price indifferent" — "either they want to buy from me or they don't; there's no comparison" (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- "Create an offer so good people would be ridiculously dumb to say no" — Hormozi-style offer mandate as negotiation leverage (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Qualification gate: web form captures budget, project type, website, and challenges before any call; no budget/no fit = no meeting (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT Sales Funnel Strategy to CRUSH B2B Sales")
- Concrete offer/price proof points: $2,000 coaching offers sold by clients with only ~31 subscribers; clients hitting 5K/10K/15K per month; work-for-free-for-a-testimonial as a fallback (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- Lead-magnet → call CTA: "DM me the keyword 'brand' and I'll send you the free 9-to-5 Personal Brand Blueprint right away" (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- ROI value framing for services: "When they pay you, they expect to make more money than they paid you — so your value is: by buying my service, I help you make more money." (Patrick Dang — "The BEST Sales Lead Generation Method")
- De-risk via milestone payment plan instead of dropping price: "pay X% upfront, then the next payment when we hit XYZ benchmark" — keeps full price, lowers perceived risk (Patrick Dang — "My ULTIMATE Negotiations Strategy")
- Concession-for-commitment: drop price only for a sign-by date or monthly→annual prepay (framed like Spotify yearly-vs-monthly: "you'd use it anyway, save 20%") (Patrick Dang — "My ULTIMATE Negotiations Strategy")
- Service pricing anchor: high-ticket service at $2-5K/month, "3-4 clients = $10K/month"; beginners should close on a call before trying landing page/DM sales (Patrick Dang — "The Most Overlooked $10K/Month Online Business" / "Beginners Guide To Making Money with Claude AI")
- Lead-magnet → call funnel: free downloadable skill/tool captures email → nurture → free limited-seat training → book-a-call; "limited seats… before spots run out" scarcity (Patrick Dang — "Beginners Guide To Making Money with Claude AI")
- Free-tier-as-offer (SaaS): lead with concrete free allowances ("25 monthly searches, 50 verifications, 500 recipients per campaign") + trust badges ("used by 3M+ professionals at Google, IBM, Microsoft, Adobe; high G2/Capterra scores") (Patrick Dang — "The ULTIMATE ChatGPT Cold Email Strategy")
- High-ticket coaching anchored at $3,000, achievable "in 8 days flat, without a website, without a personal brand, and nobody knew who he was" — proof/risk-reversal framing for a starter offer (Patrick Dang — "It's Boring, But You'll Make $3000 in Just 8 Days")
- High-ticket range as standard: "$2,000 to $5,000," sellable on as little as ~1,000 subscribers; positioned against "traditional education is not what it was" so people seek "alternative education" (Patrick Dang — "How to START a Youtube Channel in 2025")
- Free-training → book-a-call architecture: "free training that breaks down this entire process step by step… then book a call with me and my team" (Patrick Dang — "Build Your Personal Brand Empire in 2025")
- SaaS sponsor offer to swipe: "Try Pipedrive free for 14 days and get 20% off your first year." (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT B2B Sales Strategy to Close More Deals")
- Risk-reversal for a placement offer: charge thousands to "guarantee someone gets placed in a high-paying job." (Patrick Dang — "How A Personal Brand Will CHANGE Your Life in 2025")
- Proof/outcome anchor: "go from literally zero in revenue and no offer to making $10,000 per month and beyond." (Patrick Dang — "How To Generate Leads with AI in 2026")
- Free-trial CTA (lead magnet → tool access): "free trial… access to their entire database of millions of contacts, all the AI tools, plus send outbound sequences all from one platform — everything you need without duct-taping five tools together." (Patrick Dang — "How To Generate Leads with AI in 2026")
- Brand premium as pricing justification: Nike sneaker ~$7 to make, sells for $200-250; identical hoodies priced 20x apart — price is set by perceived brand value, not cost (Patrick Dang — "How A Personal Brand Will CHANGE Your Life in 2025")

### Objection handling
- "What's your pricing?" deflection (verbatim): "That depends on what you want — we offer a lot of services. Even if I gave you a price it may not be what you need, so to give a realistic price it makes sense to understand what you can work with first. Is that okay?" (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Commodity-buyer leverage (you as buyer): "Everyone's doing the same thing, it's all commodity work — this guy's charging X, can you beat it?" then make vendors bid (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS")
- Reframe against price-shopping (you as seller): if positioned as a commodity your price collapses; craft a narrative that you alone solve their pain "better and faster" so they stop comparing (Patrick Dang — "TOP Negotiation SECRETS" / "The PERFECT Sales Funnel Strategy")
- "What if my boss finds out about my side business?" → most bosses don't care if work doesn't slip; if they do, stay low-key (grow where coworkers aren't, use first-name + verb like "Patrick Builds"), and "never sell in public" (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- "My industry is too boring/saturated" → boring = less competition; sell content/coaching back into the niche you already work in (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- "I don't want to do outbound" → "Nobody knows who you are. So either you create content and they come to you, or you go to them — cold outbound still works." (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- "I have no testimonials/clients yet" → "You yourself are your first testimonial. Everybody starts from zero. You can work for free for a testimonial, but I prefer to put a price in front of people to see if they really want it." (Patrick Dang — "Why 9-5 Employees NEED To Start a Personal Brand in 2026")
- Price-too-low standoff (tonality + respect): "I totally understand you want 10K — you're a small business, not sure it'll be worthwhile, I get it. Now, 10K respectfully feels too low for what we're looking for — we'd barely make money and it wouldn't make business sense." Then pivot to de-risking levers, not caving (Patrick Dang — "My ULTIMATE Negotiations Strategy")
- "You don't always have to lower price to win — sometimes you just give up something for free to make the person feel more confident in buying." (Patrick Dang — "My ULTIMATE Negotiations Strategy")
- "Is sales sleazy?" reframe: "Amazon/Salesforce don't do hundreds of billions by lying — if they lied, no one would buy. Good salespeople aren't liars; you communicate and show value." (Patrick Dang — "Quit Your Job To Join Tech Sales?")
- "I'm a total beginner / not an expert" → "People pay for results. Businesses don't care if you use AI or not — they want results quickly and easily." (client signed multi-six-figure clients learning as he went) (Patrick Dang — "Beginners Guide To Making Money with Claude AI")
- "Will AI replace this job?" reframe for high-ticket B2B: "You won't make a million-dollar decision online without talking to a human — what if you buy the wrong thing?" so a salesperson is always needed (Patrick Dang — "Quit Your Job To Join Tech Sales?")
- Forcing the close too early backfires: pushing on call one looks "unprofessional, desperate" and pushes buyers to a competitor "who knows how to treat their customers" — respect the buying cycle (Patrick Dang — "5 B2B Sales & Business Development Mistakes To Avoid")
- Budget ask with built-in reframe: "I respect that — but it'd help because I don't want to waste your time or mine. If the budget doesn't work, there's no point continuing. Could you give me a range, just so I understand if it's a good fit on both sides?" (frames the ask as protecting THEM) (Patrick Dang — "How to Master COLD CALLING in 8 Minutes")
- "It's too early to ask budget" reframe: "No it's not — sometimes they don't know, but sometimes you get it on the first call." Always go for a range. (Patrick Dang — "How to Master COLD CALLING in 8 Minutes")
- Lost-deal lesson (qualify earlier): a deal reached negotiation with no budget → "Next time, on the first call, ask the prospect their budget so we don't waste their time or ours." (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT B2B Sales Strategy to Close More Deals")
- Failing-funnel diagnosis: "If you're reaching out to a lot of people but not scheduling demos… are you following up enough?" — locate where the cycle breaks before blaming the offer (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT B2B Sales Strategy to Close More Deals")
- Selling-in-the-DM objection: DMs don't convert because "your offer isn't good enough yet, and it's hard to sell in a DM what you've never sold on the phone." Move them to a call. (Patrick Dang — "It's Boring, But You'll Make $3000 in Just 8 Days")
- Competitor objection reframe (1-10 scale): "If you rated them 1-10, what would that be? A 7? What would need to change for them to be a 10?" — the gap they name is your opening (Patrick Dang — "3 MOST Important Skills in Sales (2025)")
- Documented objection library: keep written objections (budget, timing, need, competitors) with canned answers so any rep can pull the reframe mid-call (Patrick Dang — "3 MOST Important Skills in Sales (2025)")
- Pre-empt objections with research: use AI to predict likely objections for a company/budget before the call and pre-write counters (Patrick Dang — "Top Sales Trends To Generate More Leads & Close More Deals in 2025")
- Dispel the limiting belief: "Don't psych yourself out — these companies will give you a chance and are willing to take a chance on someone with no experience." (Patrick Dang — "How To Get A Sales Job Without Sales Experience")

### Frameworks / formulas
- Universal content/post + outreach skeleton: **Hook → Pain → Solution → Why it matters (now) → CTA** — same structure for LinkedIn post, YouTube short, IG video (Patrick Dang — "How To Escape Your 9-5 and Make More Money (in 90 days)")
- "Inbound-led outbound": create content to warm leads, then DM everyone who likes/comments/views — "create in public, give value, but sell in private." (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025" / "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- The Perfect Pitch one-page template: **Intro (story/pain stat) → Message Summary → Agenda (3 pts) → Body 1/2/3 (each = Pain → Solution → Why now) → Summary → Close.** "If you can't fit the whole pitch on one page, you don't understand it well enough." (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT Sales Pitch Guide")
- Body structure for every pitch point: **Pain → Solution → Why**, max 3 pains (1-3 is what actually moves money) (Patrick Dang — "The PERFECT Sales Pitch Guide")
- The "Belief Triangle": buyer must believe (1) in YOU, (2) in your VEHICLE/method, (3) that THEY can do it too. "Belief doesn't start on the call, it starts in your content — like propaganda." (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- Pitch-on-the-spot: ask questions → listen → collect pains → "reverse the pains into the solution. That's your pitch. Problem, solution, done." (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- Mission > Niche pyramid: **Mission (who you help + transformation) → Method (unique angle) → Momentum (products/actions).** Anchor identity to a mission so you can switch niches and keep the audience (Patrick Dang — "You Don't Need To Niche…Create a Mission Instead")
- One-sentence offer formula (two variants): "I help [avatar] get [result] without [obstacle] in [30/60/90 days]." / "I help [avatar] achieve [result] by [your unique process/mechanism]." If you can't say it in one sentence, you don't know what you do (Patrick Dang — "How To Escape Your 9-5…" / "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- B2B vs B2C buyer psychology: in B2B they want you to work FOR them; in B2C they want to BECOME you — sell each differently (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- DM opener that qualifies (A/B question): "Are you here for the content, or are you looking to [grow your business / get a high-paying job]?" (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025")
- Personalize-at-scale: pick 20 prospects in the SAME industry with the SAME problem, send the same message — "it feels personalized because it's for their industry, their specific problem, this particular time." (Patrick Dang — "How To Escape Your 9-5…")
- Follow-up rule: 1-2 sentences, just re-ping — "the chance of them responding to a follow-up is as high as the first message." (Patrick Dang — "How To Escape Your 9-5…")
- "Optimize for revenue, not followers": ask buyers "what got you to book?" and make more of THAT exact content (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025")
- Answer a question with a question: never answer a prospect's question directly until you know the intent, or you may disqualify yourself (quote 3 months when they wanted 1) (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- Challenge the customer: reframe the "current way" by asking if they could do it "better, faster, cheaper" — a satisfied prospect won't pay to change (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- Case-study story structure: subject/character → challenges → what they tried alone that failed → what you did specifically → result, tied back to the listener (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- First impression = how you look + how you sound + words you say, in that order; decision to like you happens in 2-5 seconds (Patrick Dang — "How To Prepare For A Sales Interview")
- The 4 P's of personality-driven content: Personality (worldview/beliefs), Performance (delivery/conviction), Physical appearance (distinct visual identity), Proof (results/testimonials) (Patrick Dang — "How 'Normal' People Are Blowing Up On YouTube in 2026")
- Why-customers-don't-buy diagnostic (5 blockers): bad product, doesn't solve pain, timing, budget, perceived likelihood of success — qualify against each (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone")
- Buying = **Pain × Believability**: identify the pain, then prove perceived likelihood you'll solve it — "the more you can get them to believe, the higher prices you can command" (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone")
- Pain-first presentation: open by restating their pains from discovery ("last time you said problem 1, 2, 3"), then solve each — only raise pains they told you they care about (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- Agenda framing every meeting: state goal + line items + "at the end we'll see if it makes sense to move forward — does that sound okay?"; repeat every call (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- Keep presentations 10-15 min, make it a conversation — "the more questions they ask, the more interested they are" (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- Content-trend thesis: Polished (Iman Gadzhi) → Raw (Sam Sulek) → "Effortless era" — some production but feels like you're not trying; positions against AI slop (Patrick Dang — "How 'Normal' People Are Blowing Up On YouTube in 2026")
- Differentiation via one twist: overlay one personality "flavor" on a dry expert topic (Amazon ads taught through a deep-sea-diving lens) so a boring subject stands out (Patrick Dang — "How 'Normal' People Are Blowing Up On YouTube in 2026")
- Ikigai as skill-picker: sell at the intersection of what you love, what you're good at, what the world needs, what you can be paid for (Patrick Dang — "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- 3-step monetization: (1) find a skill via ikigai, (2) make content to pull inbound, (3) make the offer and sign clients (Patrick Dang — "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- Content 80/20: agitate a specific problem, then give the solution ("Pain → Solution"). If that's the only content you made, you'd still make money (Patrick Dang — "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- Point A → Point B selling: surface where they are now, where they want to go, position your offer as the bridge; the easier the bridge, the easier the sale (Patrick Dang — "Top 5 POWERFUL Sales Questions")
- Buying-timeline close: ask how they want to be closed, write down each internal step (boss, meeting, procurement), put a date on each to co-build the timeline and shorten the cycle (Patrick Dang — "5 Closing Sales Tips")
- Nice-to-have → must-have: quantify the cost of the status quo (months of wasted employee time = tens of thousands) to flip the value prop (Patrick Dang — "5 Closing Sales Tips")
- Done-for-you vs. coaching split: do the work for them when you can (charge thousands vs. cost of a full-time hire); coach when they must do the work themselves (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A Profitable Personal Brand in 2025")
- "Solve the problem + add your personality/philosophy": the how-to makes it useful, the personal layer makes it un-copyable (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A Profitable Personal Brand in 2025")
- Niche-format arbitrage: win by doing one format in a niche where few others use it (long-form where everyone does shorts, or vice versa) (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A Profitable Personal Brand in 2025")
- 80/20 talk ratio: listen 80%, speak 20%; selling is listening and solving, not pitching (Patrick Dang — "Top 5 Qualities of Successful Salespeople")
- Cold-call "context = leverage" opener: cite a recent trigger event (new exec, funding, M&A, new product, industry trend) so you sound like an insider, not a spammer (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- Trigger-event list for personalization: new C-suite hire, won a big deal, raised funding, acquired/merged, launched a product, industry-wide trend shift (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- Sell sequence: (1) get them to like you, (2) make them feel the pain — let them vent every problem and every failed vendor, (3) pitch ONLY the slice that maps to the pains they named (Patrick Dang — "The GREATEST Money-Making Skill You Will EVER Need")
- Origin-story formula: clear point-A-to-point-B transformation; tell it over and over until people remember the STORY, not the tips. Three ingredients: authentic struggle + aspirational transformation + unique positioning via unfair advantages (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025")
- "Steak + sauce" content model: 3-4 core pillars you're known for (the steak), seasoned with personal passions/hobbies (the sauce) to stay unique and bingeable (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025" / "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- "Niche of one": stack origin story + pillars + sauce + credibility so the COMBINATION is uncopyable even if each element isn't unique (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025")
- "Make content feel like an episode in a season," not a one-off how-to, so people return for YOU (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025")
- Skill-to-Income Roadmap: 1) Offer (what/who/price) → 2) Lead Gen (brand + content + outbound) → 3) Monetization (call → conversation → fit). "If you can go through this cycle just one time, you will have your first client." (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")
- Sell-before-you-build: "Don't build anything, ask them what they want, and if they agree to pay you money, then you build it." Pair with a custom Loom of your AI workflow for that prospect (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")
- Telling Human Stories: lead with struggle/vulnerability, not wins — "It's not about who wins the fight. It's why they are in the ring in the first place." (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- Combine 3 mega-trends to be un-copyable: pick a growing trend, then stack multiple (his: personal branding + online education + AI) so you stop looking like a copycat (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- Voice-dump prompt for origin story: "You are a top 0.1% personal brand and storytelling expert… Help me write my origin story using the hero's journey…" then talk 5 min via voice transcription and repurpose to every platform (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- Niche-down formula: take a skill where you're not world-class, apply it to a high-money, low-competition niche (generic CapCut tutorials → video-editing agency for construction companies) (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Risk-reversal / ISA model (strongest in set): "There's no upfront cost. We only collect a payment once you get a full-time well-paying job — we take a percentage of your salary for a year. If it's not a fit, you don't pay a cent. We only get paid if you're successful." (Patrick Dang — "Close Over The Phone Live Sales Role Play")
- Risk-reversal ladder, weakest→strongest: money-back-if-not-done → "you don't even pay me until I do a good job" — the more risk you absorb, the more sales and higher price (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone")
- Performance/rev-share offer for no-budget prospects: "Don't pay me anything upfront. Let me double your ad budget, and I take 20% of what you make — my service is effectively free because you only pay out of the money I generate." (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone")
- Minimum-viable offer: no website needed — sell on the phone, then send a one-pager Google Doc (mission, # of calls, curriculum). "Made tens of thousands… literally off of this Google doc." (Patrick Dang — "How To Escape Your 9-5…")
- Lead magnet → multi-channel capture: free training that collects name, phone/WhatsApp, email, LinkedIn URL — "many angles to start a conversation." (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- High-ticket logic: "one $10,000 client is worth way more than a bunch of smaller clients" — sell 2K-10K, not $10-300 products; $97/mo churns and isn't worth the close effort (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand" / "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide")
- Cheap-test economics framing: "3 clients/month at 2-5K each = 10K/month — you don't need a big following, just a few customers." (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025")
- Application/qualifying form before any call: quitting 9-5 or already in business, country, LinkedIn, monthly income (budget), sole decision maker (authority), when can you start (timeline) — turns cold into warm (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025")
- Speed-as-premium: "We can get it done in one month… usually much faster than industry average, however because we're good we can do it for you — but here's the catch [price]." (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- "Perceived as free" pricing: price below the extra revenue you generate (e.g. a % of revenue) so the client reasons it costs them nothing (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A Profitable Personal Brand in 2025")
- Value-stacking math: "Give me $100K, I give you $150K back, every time — how many times can you sell that? Infinite." Sell value greater than price ($1 in, $2 back) (Patrick Dang — "Top Sales SECRETS" / "5 Closing Sales Tips")
- Charge higher, not cheaper: racing to the bottom kills margins and service quality; higher margins fund better talent and a service competitors "literally can't compete" with (Patrick Dang — "Top Sales SECRETS")
- Specificity premium: "If you're selling to everybody, you're not selling to anyone." More specific avatar + mechanism = higher price (Patrick Dang — "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- Pricing as a test: reverse-engineer target lifetime value per client, then keep pitching the offer until people say yes (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A Profitable Personal Brand in 2025")
- Credibility-by-association proof: name-drop where past customers ended up ("Oracle, Salesforce, Fastly") to make the result feel real and attainable (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- Risk-reversal by honest carve-out: "I can't guarantee you'll get the job — that's on you — but I CAN guarantee I'll give you the best knowledge based on my and my students' experience." Guarantee only what you control (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- Keep it simple to start: one avatar, one product, one price point, one lead-gen channel, one closing method — repeat before building tiers (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025")
- Pricing ramp for beginners: do it free for first testimonials, then start at $2-3K, build to $5K+; "1 client/week at $3-5K = $12-20K/mo." (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide" / "DON'T Start a Personal Brand")
- Offer architecture example: "FounderX" yearly membership bundling coaching + info product + community (recurring fixed fee, not monthly low-ticket) (Patrick Dang — "The ONLY Personal Brand Guide You Need in 2025")
- Land-and-expand pricing: scope at "at least $3,000/month" ("fair for you, fair for them"), then upsell scope → renegotiate to $5,500/mo; ~$25K total contract (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")
- Program CTA architecture: free training → "if it's a fit, apply to book a call" → scarcity "I only take a limited number of clients every month" + bonus stack (all AI prompts in a Google Doc template) (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- Founder/scarcity framing: "right now there's a waitlist… you'll be one of the first members." (Patrick Dang — "The NEW Way To Generate Leads in 2025")

### Objection handling
- Soft-close to surface objections: "Is there anything else you need to see before making a decision?" / "What would it take for you to become a client of ours?" (Patrick Dang — "Close Over The Phone Live Sales Role Play")
- Feel-Felt-Found / "time" reframe: "Many of our students felt the same way… what they found is that usually time isn't the main factor, it's priorities. It's not whether you have enough time — it's whether you actually want to do this." (Patrick Dang — "Close Over The Phone Live Sales Role Play")
- "Can't afford it" → flip to risk-free: "That's fair, it's an investment — do you mind if I share how it works?" then reveal the pay-after-you-succeed structure so price evaporates (Patrick Dang — "Close Over The Phone Live Sales Role Play")
- Probe before answering: "What's stopping you from moving forward?" / "What exactly about the program do you feel may not work for you?" — diagnose, then reframe (Patrick Dang — "Close Over The Phone Live Sales Role Play")
- Surface the hidden ("black swan") objection at close: "You sound excited, but a lot of times people sound excited and then ghost me — I'm not saying you'll do that, but is there any reason you'd want to work with us?" (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- Stacked close: squash the objection, then "Now that that's out of the way, is there anything ELSE preventing you moving forward?" — repeat until "no," then "So would you say you're ready to make a decision now?" (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- "I don't know" response: "Great question — let me check with my team to give you the proper answer. Is it okay if I get back to you on that?" (Patrick Dang — "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- Shorten the timeline via question, not pressure: "I totally respect the six-month timeline — just curious, what's stopping you from doing it this month? If I were in your shoes I'd prioritize it because it'd do X, Y, Z." Let them reach urgency themselves (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone" / "TOP 5 Sales Pitch Tips")
- "No budget yet": confirm when budget opens, then "Since you're going to buy software anyway, let me show you how this works so when the time comes you have everything to decide." (Patrick Dang — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone")
- Reframe DIY objection with future-cost questions: "Have you ever built a sales org before? So how long would that take? 3-6 months for industry average — why not do it faster?" → "We don't know how" opens the sale (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- Reframe "what we have is working": "It's great this is working, but what if everything gets shut down and nobody's walking by — can your business survive?" — introduce risk to motivate change (Patrick Dang — "Top 3 Sales Techniques To Close More Deals")
- DIY objection ("I can do it myself"): "What's stopping you from reaching your goals on your own? If you could've, you wouldn't be on this call." Make them verbally admit the blocker (Patrick Dang — "Top 5 POWERFUL Sales Questions")
- Let the prospect sell themselves: "What were you hoping I could do to help?" / "What got you interested in our call today?" — they articulate the pain and solution so you barely pitch (Patrick Dang — "Top 5 POWERFUL Sales Questions")
- Handle objections EARLY, not at the end: surface budget/fit up front so there are "no objections left" at the ask (Patrick Dang — "5 Closing Sales Tips" / "Top Sales SECRETS")
- Respect-the-buying-process objection: don't hard-close enterprise on call one — "Why are you pushing so hard? You're not respecting our process." backfires (Patrick Dang — "5 Closing Sales Tips")
- "We already work with a competitor" → challenge the status quo ("Would it make sense to replace that vendor with someone who gets better results?") or position as a complement, not a head-to-head replacement (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- Reframe objections as gifts: they tell you, in the prospect's own words, why they won't buy — free intel to fix messaging/offer. "Objections are your best friend." (Patrick Dang — "Cold Calling Techniques That Really Work")
- "How's it going today sounds fake" → it works when delivered with mastered tonality; ~70% of why someone likes you on a cold call is tonality, not words (Patrick Dang — "How to ACCELERATE Your Cold Call Skills")
- Reframe rejection: expect ~95% no / 5% yes; chase the "no" to qualify out fast; never accept a "maybe" (yes = sell, no = move on, maybe = wasted time) (Patrick Dang — "How To Get Over The Fear of Cold Calling")
- Status reframe to kill call reluctance: YOU are the prize — "how lucky is this person to receive your call," not "please listen to me." (Patrick Dang — "How To Get Over The Fear of Cold Calling")
- Posture/non-desperation prevents objections: "If they buy, they buy. If they don't, they don't… come in with that confidence and you become magnetic. Come in desperate and no one buys." (Patrick Dang — "How to Build A $100K Personal Brand in 2025")
- "Not qualified" → reframe as fear, not capability: "It wasn't that Sandy wasn't qualified. She was just afraid of the unknown." (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")
- "I'm not an AI expert" → "Every person in AI didn't know anything about AI just a year or two ago… put your head down and grind for 6 months and you'll be one of the top five voices." (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")
- "I'm not the top expert" → "The world doesn't need more heroes. It needs more relatable human beings… as long as you're one step ahead of somebody, you provide value." (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- "Starting from zero subscribers" → "everybody starts from zero. But you just have to have a strong narrative and positioning." (Patrick Dang — "how i built a $100k+ personal brand using AI")
- "I haven't built it yet" → sell the promise first: "She never even built this automation… she only made a promise, made them feel confident she could do it, and then when the time came to deliver, she learned." (Patrick Dang — "I Helped a Stranger Build a 1-Person AI Business")

### Hooks / headlines / subject lines

- "Would you like to have more people desire to buy more things from you with less effort from you?" — yes-ladder opening question (Myron Golden — "How To Stop Talking Prospects Out Of Buying From You")
- "Apple did something that no other company in the history of the world will ever have the opportunity to do." — curiosity open-loop, repeated to hold attention (Myron Golden — "Secrets From Apple's Three Trillion Dollar Playbook")
- "Have you ever thought social media was stupid? I have." — relatable contrarian admission as hook (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- "Last year our business did just under $13 million in sales with $0 spent on ads." — specific proof-number hook (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- "When you read the 4-Hour Work Week, did you wonder if it was real?" — hook off a shared skepticism (Myron Golden — "Youtube Channel Makes 6 Figures In 4 hours A Week")
- "A thousand songs in your pocket" — benefit-as-name; clarity beats spec-speak (Myron Golden — "Secrets From Apple's Three Trillion Dollar Playbook")

### Frameworks / formulas
- Price-justification formula: price is justified by a **Measurable, Desirable, Stateable** outcome the prospect wants — clear before→after, desirable to THEM not you, sayable in one soundbite. "Clarity trumps clever every single time." (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- Price on the RESULT, not by analogy to competitors — "stop basing your price on what other people who teach this charge; base it on the result you can get." (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- Anchor a low-ticket offer to your high-ticket rate: "$30 book = 2 hours of my coaching; my coaching was $25k/hr = $50k of value." Always give them something to compare it to. (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- "You sell like you buy" — become a happy/generous buyer and tipper to attract happy buyers; "everything reproduces after its own kind." (Myron Golden — "How To Stop Talking Prospects Out Of Buying From You")
- Apple's 3-page playbook: (1) you're in the business of **acquiring customers**, not selling widgets — just get them to buy *something* first; (2) **AWE** customers — turn a solution into an experience (form + function → fanatical fans); (3) operate from first principles, not analogy. (Myron Golden — "Secrets From Apple's Three Trillion Dollar Playbook")
- Audience = root word "audio" = people who show up to hear from you; they pay with **attention before assets** — bigger attention pool = bigger future-buyer pool. (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- Dunbar 7-11: ~7 interactions + 11 hours of attention (or 11 + 7) before someone knows/likes/trusts you enough to buy. (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- Process goal beats vanity goal: build content to "get good at making content people want to watch," not to chase subscriber counts. (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets" / "Youtube Channel Makes 6 Figures In 4 hours A Week")
- Platform roles: Facebook = ads + groups; Instagram = impulse buyers (infomercial medium); YouTube = premium/long-form buyers + biggest audience leverage; LinkedIn = corporate; TikTok = young. (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- Boss Moves offer stack: audience-building (prerequisite) → lead-gen offer → core/lead-conversion offer ($20–$3k) → customer-ascension (premium) → continuity (recurring). (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- Make money FASTER, not just more: "turn your annual income into your monthly income" — wealth is measured in time; a million in 1 year = 20× richer than a million in 20 years. (Myron Golden — "How To Stop Talking Prospects Out Of Buying From You")
- "Money is a tool to be used, not a pool to be viewed" — cash flow over accumulation; "cash flowing is cash growing" (Dead Sea = inlet, no outlet). (Myron Golden — "Multiple Streams For Millionaire Dreams")

### VOC language
- "I'm just looking." — the reflexive wall prospects throw up at any salesperson. (Myron Golden — "How To Stop Talking Prospects Out Of Buying From You")
- "It doesn't make sense to you — it makes sense to the people who are looking for you." (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")
- "Nobody cares about your story — nobody but you and your mom." Sell what the market desires, not what you desire them to have. (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- "If people who are looking for your solution find you, that's worlds better than you finding them." (Myron Golden — "7 Figure Social Media Secrets")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Set a price you're "willing to work for whether or not people buy" — if they won't pay it, you're unwilling to do the work; that's how you find your price. Break the addiction to "yes." (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- Premium positioning: "We're not building a Walmart brand, we're building a Neiman Marcus brand." Don't discount to match the market if it clashes with your brand — "a Rolls Royce at Walmart doesn't fit." (Myron Golden — "Secrets From Apple's Three Trillion Dollar Playbook" / "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- Raise price the instant market proof shows up: $3k→$4k→$35k as buyers kept coming; $5k/hr → $25k/hr mid-call after a client's $5M day. Let the result, not your comfort, set the ceiling. (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")

### Objection handling
- "Your price is too high" → value reframe: no price is too high when the measurable/desirable/stateable result is there; no price is low enough when it isn't. (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")
- "You cost more than your competitors" → stop comparing to competitors (analogy); compare to the ROI you deliver and to your own higher-priced offers. (Myron Golden — "High Ticket Sales Price Justification")

### Objection handling

### Objection handling
- **Price objection** → "you think price is why people say yes or no — it's not. People say yes when they understand what you do and believe you can give them something they desire. If value > cost, they pay." Prove it with results ("a guy bought a $30 book and made $800k in two months") (Myron Golden — "The Answer To, 'What Do You Do'", "How To Become The Greatest Sales Person In The World").
- **"Is it good for everybody?"** → "anything that's for everybody is also for nobody… even if it would be good for everybody, it's still not good for everybody" — justifies narrow targeting (Myron Golden — "The Answer To, 'What Do You Do'").
- **Low-pressure / take-away close:** "I'm not looking for business, I'm not hoping you'll do business with me — I become the person who can produce the result, and when you're ready you'll let me know. When you know, you know" (Myron Golden — "The Answer To, 'What Do You Do'").
- **"Money can't buy happiness"** → agree, don't fight it: "happiness is all perspective; more money just gives more choices — it doesn't make you happier or sadder" (Myron Golden — "Why Money Can't Buy Happiness").
- **Selling-is-needy reframe:** "Selling is not convincing — when you try to convince, you come across as needy, and nobody buys from a needy person." Play hard-to-get (boy-meets-girl) (Myron Golden — "How To Become The Greatest Sales Person In The World").
- **Counterintuitive-offer objection:** "when something will really change your life, the first time you see it, it's so counterintuitive it seems nonsensical" — preempts "this doesn't make sense" (Myron Golden — "How One Of My Clients Grew His Business From 3 Million To 10 Million In A Year").
- **Serve who WANTS it, not who NEEDS it:** "the people who need it most often want it least; you stay stuck talking to the wrong people about the wrong thing." The seller's own scarcity belief blocks the buyer's yes ("if that thought's not in your head, it's not in your head for your clients") (Myron Golden — "How One Of My Clients Grew His Business From 3 Million To 10 Million In A Year").
- **"Selling feels icky"** → "selling isn't something you do TO people, it's something you do FOR them; when you're good, the buyer didn't do you a favor — you did them one." You feel icky because you're a terrible buyer and assume everyone else is — flip it by becoming the world's best buyer (Myron Golden — "Selling Is Easy When You Do It Like This!").
- **"Trying to GET people to buy is itself why people don't buy"** — it creates resistance ("what are you trying to get from me?"). Instead make yourself *findable* for people who already want what you sell. "What do you sell?" → "Depends — what do you want to buy?" (Myron Golden — "Selling Is Easy When You Do It Like This!").
- **Persistence vs "it's not working":** "All work works — let it work ON me until it works FOR me; you just haven't yet found your average" (Myron Golden — "Selling Is Easy When You Do It Like This!").
- **"It's too expensive"** → "It's not too expensive — you can't afford it. If it's too expensive the problem is IT and you can't fix it; if you can't afford it the problem is YOU and you can fix you." Replace "I can't afford it" with "How can I afford this? Who do I have to be?" "Buy what you desire, not the price" (Myron Golden — "Seven Mindset Shifts That Made Me Millions", "The Success Easy Button = Hard To Push").
- **"What if I don't know how?"** → "You didn't know how to walk, talk, read, or ride a bike either — not knowing has never stopped you, and there's more how-to info now than ever" (Myron Golden — "The More You Learn The More You Earn").
- **Price objection → reframe to a bigger, irrecoverable cost:** "you can't justify flying private but you can justify wasting six hours of your time… you can get the money back, you can't get the time back" (Myron Golden — "Turn Your Articulation Into Compensation").
- **"Won't free content cannibalize sales?"** → "the exact opposite is true — give away a lot of really good value and people buy from you to the tune of way more money" (Myron Golden — "Turn Your Articulation Into Compensation").
- **Money-shame** → permission + honesty: "it's okay to be rich; it doesn't make you better, just richer." Say "I don't care the MOST about money" instead of "I don't care about money" (a lie if you spend 8–12 hrs/day on it) (Myron Golden — "A Simple Formula To Make MILLIONS").
- **Pressure/desperation** → serve, don't chase: "when they feel pursued, chased, pressured, they resist… when they feel served, like you have their best interest, the only thing they can't do is not buy" (Myron Golden — "Selling Without Selling").
- **Sales-is-immoral** → moral-duty reframe: "if I've got something good, I have a moral obligation to sell it to as many people as possible"; believing in your cause gives a "five-time advantage," like a defending army over a conflicted competitor (Myron Golden — "Myron Golden In Your Corner Interview", "The Financial Statement Of Jesus Christ Pt 2").
- **"Just pray for you" vs real help:** James 2 — telling a destitute person "be warmed and filled" without meeting the need does no good; being rich lets you actually help (Myron Golden — "Myron Golden In Your Corner Interview").
- **No-pressure disarmer before a CTA:** "there's no compulsion in anything I'm saying, I'm just making you aware… then don't buy the book and don't buy the challenge" (Myron Golden — "If You Want To Get Rich Follow These Rules").
- **Disruption/fear reframes:** "disruption always follows intention — obstacles usually mean you're going the right way"; "pain is not an input from the body, it's an output from the brain — a freak-out mechanism warning you off the only thing that can transform you"; fear (real, present danger) vs anxiety (imagined, future danger) (Myron Golden — "One Hour Of Myron Motivation", "How To Get Unstuck In Life").

- Four offer types every business must master: lead-generation offers (someone to sell to) → core-product offers (the main thing) → premium-value offers (your profit center) → continuity offers (stabilize/compound). ### Objection handling
- **"That sounds like manipulation":** "If you're grown and broke, you've already been manipulated — they told me what they desire; I know I can help them get it." (Myron Golden — "How I Close Million Dollar Sales 1 On 1")
- **Pre-answer objections:** "An objection is an infected question that didn't get answered in the presentation — like an open wound that didn't get cleaned." Keep asking "What other questions?" until none. (Myron Golden — "How I Close Million Dollar Sales 1 On 1")
- **Never say "interested":** "'Interested' is a kiss-of-death word — it asks for commitment before providing value." Replace "If I could show you a way…" with "If there WERE a way…" (removes you and them from it). (Myron Golden — "How I Close Million Dollar Sales 1 On 1")
- **Payment close that bypasses "do you want to buy":** "Most people pay with Visa, Mastercard, Amex, or Discover — which will you be using to get started today?" (Myron Golden — "How I Close Million Dollar Sales 1 On 1")
- **Embedded-command close:** "If you could benefit from both sooner or later, would you choose later, or would you choose sooner?" — order so "sooner" lands last (recency). (Myron Golden — "How I Close Million Dollar Sales 1 On 1")
- **Sell only what they already want:** "Stop trying to get them to buy stuff YOU want them to buy" (steakhouse-server analogy: don't change their order into something you can understand). (Myron Golden — "Answers To Business…" / "How To Turn What You Love…")
- **"It costs too much" reframe:** read the menu left to right (the value), not right to left (the price); say "that costs more than I want to pay" or ask "how CAN I afford it?" (Myron Golden — "Answers To Business And Financial Challenges")
- **Price vs value:** "Poor people know the cost of everything and the value of nothing. Stop being a price shopper, start being a value shopper." (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Time More Valuable")
- **"I can't learn it" reframe:** "You landed on this planet unable to walk, talk, or tell time — there's nothing you can't learn. Look in the rearview mirror of your life." (Myron Golden — "The Craziest Facts I Know")
- **"I can't afford to hire someone":** "For a 7-figure business at 40 hrs/wk you're worth $500/hr, so hiring at $10/hr is 2% of you — it costs more NOT to hire than to hire." (Myron Golden — "Scaling to 8 Figures with Virtual Assistants")
- **"I want a guarantee":** "Middle-class and poor people want a guarantee; rich people want an opportunity." (Myron Golden — "How Rich People Think About Money")
- **"It's too expensive" — cost of ignorance:** a $600 battery he skipped cost him a $21,000 engine. "If you think knowledge is expensive, try ignorance." (Myron Golden — "If You Think Knowledge Is Expensive, Try Ignorance")
- **"Pay for speed":** "First 10 years we paid for experience (trial and error); now I pay for speed — for the knowledge, the time, the people." (Myron Golden — "Scaling to 8 Figures with Virtual Assistants")
- **"Circumstances are against me":** "There are contributing factors (outside, no control) and determining factors (inside, full control). It matters more WHO you are when something happens than WHAT happens." (Myron Golden — "Gas Is Up Stocks Are Down")

### Frameworks / formulas
- **4 C's of thumbnail/headline titles:** Curiosity, Contrast, Conflict, Controversy — every title carries some (not all). "Why Evil People Are Rich" = curiosity + contrast + conflict + controversy. (Myron Golden — "$ix Figures My First Year As A YouTuber…")
- **Use a question word to make a statement** — open with how/why but don't ask a question; it forces readers to ask *themselves*, so they must click. "How they programmed you to be poor." (Myron Golden — "$ix Figures My First Year As A YouTuber…")
- **Title hierarchy:** thumbnail title, headline, and platform title should NOT repeat — the headline *clarifies the thumbnail and intensifies* the curiosity/contrast/conflict/controversy. Thumbnail = Cliff Notes; title = magnifier. (Myron Golden — "$ix Figures My First Year As A YouTuber…")
- **The 30-second rule:** if 75%+ of viewers are still watching at 0:30, the algorithm rewards you — engineer the opening hook obsessively. Open-loop tactic: "tell them what the thing DID, not what the thing IS." (Myron Golden — "$ix Figures My First Year As A YouTuber…")
- **6-step content formula (ASK+DDDD):** 1) Uncover their motivation, 2) Declare their transformation, 3) Demonstrate authentication ("documentation beats conversation"), 4) Develop their imagination (with pictures), 5) Dial in your articulation (sales message), 6) Deploy confirmation. (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Content More Appealing")
- **Show payoff before process:** "If you show people the process before the payoff, all you're doing is telling them it's hard" → they go look for easy. Present solutions in their most simplistic form. (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Content More Appealing")
- **VOC research method:** Ask "What's the single biggest challenge you're having with X?" — *singular* forces a short answer people will give; tally repeated answers → that becomes your content outline / offer. (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Content More Appealing")
- **Selling = helping people make a decision they already desire to make, for their own reasons** (vs. convincing = getting someone to decide what *you* want for *your* reasons). (Myron Golden — "Sell This Way & Have People Thanking You")
- **Sell FOR people, not TO people** — discovery-led: ask enough questions that the prospect provides the *content* of the sale; you provide the *context*; then show your offer as the shortest path to their stated outcome. (Myron Golden — "Sell This Way & Have People Thanking You")
- **Wealth formula:** High Value × Low Volume = Wealth, or Low Value × High Volume = Wealth; best is High Value × High Volume. Low-value/high-volume front end → high-value/low-volume back end. (Myron Golden — "Creating Wealth Pt 2")
- **4 offer types every business must master:** lead-generation, core-product, premium-value, continuity offers. Relying on one = "one client loss or one shift in the economy away from losing your entire business." (Myron Golden — "Business Mastery Secrets" / "Fix One Thing And Make Millions")
- **Scale by the math:** leads × conversion rate × price point = revenue; raise the neglected lever ("leg day") rather than the part you enjoy. (Myron Golden — "Fix One Thing And Make Millions")
- **Product beats service for scale:** a service ties revenue to time (limited); a product (book, course, membership) is made once and sells infinitely — "it takes me no longer to sell a thousand than to sell one." Productize a service by putting it in a book/membership. (Myron Golden — "Business Mastery Secrets" / "Profitable Answers…")
- **Be → Do → Have:** become the person who can do the thing, so you can have the result. Counter to "if it's not working, try harder." "If you don't like the output, change the input." (Myron Golden — "How To Become The Best Of The Best" / "Profitable Answers…")
- **Make them define the term:** when hit with a loaded label or vague objection, make them define it first — collapses weak arguments (Elon's "Can you name one example?"). (Myron Golden — "'You Just Lied' Elon Musk…")
- **Attract-and-repel positioning:** "Anything that is for everybody is also for nobody." Let your message repel as much as it attracts. (Myron Golden — "$ix Figures…" / "Profitable Answers…")
- **Tiny Challenge (beginner coach model):** 5 one-on-one calls over 5 consecutive days, 30–45 min — no list, no tech, 100% show rate, reciprocity sells; pitch a $3K–$5K offer on call 4–5. (Myron Golden — "The Best Business Model for Beginner Coaches")
- **The wealth wheel:** (1) set a new income target above what you live on, (2) generate the income, (3) invest the *surplus* into yourself/business/cash-flow assets — never spend the cushion or you're "back at zero." Surplus into yourself/biz = tax deduction. (Grant Cardone — "You Don't Need More Money. You Need THIS Mindset")
- **Urgency is a product.** Without manufactured urgency it's nearly impossible to move comfortable people to act; invent small controllable deadlines ("a Friday") to manufacture momentum. (Grant Cardone — "The Urgency Shift That Changes Everything")
- **3 reasons reps fail to set meetings:** (1) they don't nail the first 15 seconds / lack a proven opener; (2) can't overcome objections; (3) no compelling call-to-action. (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **Cold call opener structure:** "Hey, this is [Name] from [Company], how are you? The reason I'm giving you a call is…" then tailor the reason by seniority (low-level → "ring a bell?"; exec → "I noticed you oversee [role]…is [outcome] a priority?"). (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **Two categories of objections:** (1) up-front rejection before your pitch (hard); (2) post-ask objection after you request time (easy). Treat them differently. (Trent Dressel — "Cold Call Objection Handling Scripts & Responses")
- **Objection-handling formula:** Validate/acknowledge (say it back differently so they feel heard) → give a compelling reason it still makes sense → re-ask. (Trent Dressel — "Cold Call Objection Handling Scripts & Responses")
- **Best-case/worst-case CTA + assumptive close:** "Best case we continue the conversation; worst case there's no alignment and we part ways." Then mirror their priority and assume the meeting: "I'm available tomorrow at 2pm, how does that work?" (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **Buyer loss-aversion frame:** corporate buyers "fear loss more than they love gain" — they play not to lose money, not to lose their job, not to look stupid. Sell safety/ROI: "it'll be a slam dunk." (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **Articulate their problem better than they can:** before writing copy, get into the buyer's world, daily tasks, and the metrics they're judged on. "You build trust if you can articulate their problem as well as they can or better." (Trent Dressel — "The Future of Tech Sales")

- **Hot-seat / audience leverage:** charge one person $5K to be coached one-on-one *on the condition* others may watch ("otherwise it's $25K with no one watching") — one such challenge did ~$290K. (Myron Golden — "The Best Business Model…")
- **Myron's product ladder (real numbers):** $20–30 books; $97/$297/$797 tickets; $1K & $3K courses; coaching at $27K/$55K/$350K/$1M-yr. Books+tickets ~$300K/mo, premium ~$800K/mo, continuity ~$200K/mo. "Boss Moves" $30 book → $35K–70K/mo. (Myron Golden — "Fix One Thing And Make Millions" / "Profitable Answers…")
- **Books as front-end ascension offers:** cheap books ($75–80 total) sold to those who can't yet afford the $5K–$55K programs; they apply it, make money, come back and buy. (Myron Golden — "Profitable Answers…")

- **Fee structure as risk-reversal:** "1% in, 1% out, 1% to manage, 20% on the promote," plus an **8% preferred return** to the investor first; proof stack: "$600M distributed in real cash, $800M in tax write-offs, 76 deals, Fund One 47% net of fees." (Grant Cardone — "Cardone Capital Fees EXPOSED")
- **Comparison anchoring:** "Vanguard makes ¾ of 1% on $11T, Blackstone 1.5% on $2T" — frames his fees as reasonable. (Grant Cardone — "Cardone Capital Fees EXPOSED")
- **No-budget, no-risk meeting offer:** "We're not talking money today… I just want to give your team a cost-savings proposal." Worst case they leave with new data, best case the conversation continues. (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")

### Objection handling
- **"My content is being shadowbanned":** "99.9% of the time your account isn't shadowbanned — your content just isn't grabbing and holding attention. If suppression were real, Mr. Beast and teenage influencers wouldn't exist." (Myron Golden — "How To Make Content So Good…")
- **"Nobody cares about my content/story":** "Nobody's watching your content for you — they don't like you that much. Nobody wants to read your story unless it shows them how to create their own glory." (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Content More Appealing")
- **"I'm not good at speaking/writing":** "The reason you're not good is you don't do it — and you don't do it because you think you're not good. Do it more and you'll get better." (Myron Golden — "How To Make Your Content More Appealing")
- **"More money will fix my money problems":** "Making more money with the same mindset won't make you richer — it'll multiply and amplify your money problems." (Myron Golden — "Regardless Of Your Income…")
- **"Try harder":** "Some of the worst advice that could exist — putting more time and effort into what's already proven not to work." Fix who you're being, not the effort. (Myron Golden — "How To Become The Best Of The Best")
- **"Is selling pushy?" (moral-license close):** Proverbs 11:26 — "He that withholdeth the corn, the people shall curse him." If you have something good, you have a *moral obligation* to sell it to as many as possible. (Myron Golden — "Sell This Way…")
- **"They didn't really sell me, I just bought it":** "Everything you've ever bought, somebody sold it to you — even the iPhone. Great selling just feels like buying what you already wanted." (Myron Golden — "Sell This Way…")
- **"Is it worth it?" (value vs. cost):** "Poor people know the cost of everything and the value of nothing; rich people know the value of everything and the cost of nothing. - **"It's too hard / too risky":** "Downside is limited, upside is unlimited — that's a chance I'm always willing to take. The people who have the most to lose are the least afraid to lose it." (Myron Golden — "Get Motivated For Millions In 2024")
- **"It's not working yet":** "All work works — heads it works *for* you, tails it works *on* you, until you become the person it can work for. It wasn't working — keyword: yet." (Myron Golden — "Get Motivated…" / "Profitable Answers…")
- **Trolls/haters:** "Never argue with an idiot — they'll drag you to their level and beat you with experience. Your haters are your elevators." (Myron Golden — "'You Just Lied' Elon Musk…" / "$ix Figures…")
- **Takeaway/negative sell:** "This deal is closed, fully funded — you can't put your money in. I'm not pitching you." Removing the offer raises desire and signals honesty. (Grant Cardone — "Cardone Capital Fees EXPOSED")
- **Permission to walk:** "If you think it's unfair, don't do it. If you don't trust me, you should not invest with me." Disqualification that builds trust. (Grant Cardone — "Cardone Capital Fees EXPOSED")
- **"He's just getting rich off us" (align self-interest):** "You should *want* your partners to make a lot of money — the more he makes investors, the more they invest." (Grant Cardone — "Cardone Capital Fees EXPOSED")
- **"I'm about to jump in a meeting / why are you calling?"** → "I know I'm calling you out of the blue — may I have 30 seconds to tell you the reason why I'm calling?" (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **"We already have something in place"** → "I don't expect your team to change anytime soon. I just want to give you a cost-savings proposal interesting enough to take back to your current supplier — maybe get a better price." (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **"Send me an email"** → "Happy to — actually, I find emails usually aren't the best use of your time. It'd be more valuable to set up a quick intro; if there's alignment we continue, if not we part ways." (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **"We have no budget"** → "Definitely not looking for budget today. It'd seem you'd care about a solution that drives the most impact — by the end you'll either feel more confident in what you have, or see a big area of opportunity." (Trent Dressel — "Cold Call Objection Handling Scripts")
- **"We're using your competitor"** → reframe as positive: "It's better when they already use a solution — it validates they have money and care to spend on this." Acknowledge, then ask for the meeting. (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")
- **"We just renewed"** → "No problem at all. Maybe there's a point when you renew, or maybe there's something your program is missing today." Play the long game for a future meeting. (Trent Dressel — "How to Cold Call Strangers")

### Frameworks / formulas
- **Canonical B2B cold-call opening** (surfaced across ~5 videos): "Hey [Name], this is Trent from [Company], how are you?" → pause + listen → "The reason I'm calling you *specifically* is because you lead [role] at [company]" → state an *outcome* they must care about (not a feature) → leading qualification Q → handle objection → ask for the meeting. The "reason I'm calling you specifically" anchor is mandatory — it settles the prospect's subconscious "who is this / why me." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play" / "The BEST Cold Call Opening Line" / "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD")
- **Permission micro-ask** (the single most-repeated tactic): "I know I'm calling you out of the blue — may I have 30 seconds to tell you the reason why I'm calling?" Works ~80–90% of the time; buys 30 more seconds and disarms any opening brush-off. (Trent Dressel — "I Cold Call for a living" / "Sell Like a Champ" / "The Best Cold Call Script Ever")
- **Email-before-dial sequence**: always send an email first so your name + company sit in their inbox; the call then opens warm with "does the name [company] ring a bell?" (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script for B2B/Software Sales")
- **"How are you?" diagnostic**: ask and pause — "I'm okay, how are you?" = green light to run your talk track; "Who are you?" = irritable, get to the point fast. (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play")
- **Absurd-yes priority question**: frame the qualifier so a "no" is almost impossible — "Is [employee engagement / feedback] a priority for you and the team this year?" → "Well, of course it is." (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script for B2B/Software Sales")
- **Value-prop = outcomes, not features**: "We help you [collect employee feedback in the moments that matter] to drive outcomes such as lowering attrition, improving productivity, improving engagement." (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script for B2B/Software Sales")
- **Pitch-the-company formula**: "[Company] helps [buyer persona] solve [problem], which leads to [negative consequence], by [how you provide value]." (Trent Dressel — "10 Sales Job Interview Questions and Answers")
- **End-of-call agenda script** (lowers pressure, raises show rate): "My objective for our meeting is to discuss your priorities, introduce how we might help, and if we both agree there's alignment I'd like to continue — if not, we can part ways. How does that sound?" (Trent Dressel — "I Cold Call for a living" / "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD")
- **Risk-reversal two-outcome close**: "By the end of our call you'll either feel all the more confident in your existing partner, or feel certainty that our team could bring additional value to yours." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- **Cold-Call Moneyball metrics** (reverse-engineer dials from target): Answer rate ~6–8% → Set rate ~15–18% → Show rate ~70–80% → Conversion ~90%. ~1,000 calls ≈ 60 convos ≈ 15 meetings ≈ 8–9 shows ≈ 7 qualified opps. "You can't improve what you don't measure." (Trent Dressel — "A Rough Quarter Ahead for Cold Calling" / "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD" / "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- **8-Point daily pipeline OS**: 8–10 prospects added = 1pt; 5–8 custom emails = 1pt; 1 live conversation = 1pt; 1 meeting set = 1pt; 1 qualified opp = 1pt; 30 min self-development = 1pt. "Nobody who consistently hits 8 points a day has ever missed quota." (Trent Dressel — "A Rough Quarter Ahead for Cold Calling" / "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- **Show-rate booster sequence**: confirm email on the call → state the agenda live → send the calendar invite immediately → send a "Call Reminder" email the night before reaffirming agenda + a value deposit. (Trent Dressel — "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD")
- **MEDDICC discovery**: Metric, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Competition, Champion, Compelling event — "it's a puzzle; the more you fill out, the higher your win rate." (Trent Dressel — "How To Run A Discovery Call (Best Sales Questions)")
- **BANT + amplify the implication**: reduce "Need" to pain, then amplify the *consequence* of the pain — scratch → infection → losing the arm. (Trent Dressel — "3 Easy Steps to RUIN A Sales Career")
- **"Why now?" = the compelling event**: named the single biggest urgency driver; keep dragging the prospect back to it to push the deal to signature. (Trent Dressel — "How To Run A Discovery Call")
- **Champion vs. cheerleader test**: a real champion has influence AND sells on your behalf — test them by asking them to do things and watching what actually gets done. (Trent Dressel — "How To Run A Discovery Call")
- **"Sell the time, not the product"**: the cold call's only job is to set the meeting — don't feature-dump, don't run full BANT; pique curiosity (stories drive business) and give a reason to meet. (Trent Dressel — "I'm officially cold calling again!" / "Things I Learned from 53,000 Cold Calls")
- **Tone over script**: "What you say isn't as important as how you say it" — tone, pitch, inflection, pauses. Practice by recording your pitch on your phone and listening back. If the call feels rushed, *you're* rushing it. (Trent Dressel — "3 Best Cold Calling Tips" / "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD")
- **Force the calendar invite**: never accept "follow up with me" — "What day works best for you?" → get a day → "Perfect, I'll send the invite now," then confirm the email live. (Trent Dressel — "3 Best Cold Calling Tips" / "Live B2B Cold Call")
- **Account/territory tiering**: Top ~10 accounts = do anything to break in (fly to HQ, events, hyper-custom touch) → next ~50 = lighter touch → ~75–125 = automated/SDR-partnered. Focus where revenue and prospect-gain are highest. (Trent Dressel — "I'm officially cold calling again!")
- **3–4x pipeline coverage rule**: to hit quota carry 3–4x that in pipeline, then reverse-engineer to daily calls/emails. (Trent Dressel — "How I Structure My Sales Day" / "3 Easy Steps to RUIN A Sales Career")
- **Minimum-deal pre-qualify**: "It's going to cost ~$10K — is that realistic?" If no, "then we're not the right fit." (Caveat: take a smaller land if the account has expansion potential.) (Trent Dressel — "I'm struggling to perform right now")
- **Goal-laddering**: tie the prospect's personal goals → department goals → company initiatives, and show how you drive a business outcome at the top of that ladder — that's how spend gets justified. (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script")
- **AI-era buyer "safe-bet" 4 factors**: buyers de-risk toward (1) well-funded/established vendors, (2) shorter contracts (1-yr over 3-yr for CFO sign-off), (3) fast time-to-value on immediate pain, (4) low data/privacy risk. (Trent Dressel — "How AI Could End Tech Sales As We Know It")

### VOC language
- Opening brush-offs / gatekeeping (master list): "Who is this?" / "How'd you get my number?" / "Are you trying to sell something?" / "Are you a telemarketer/solicitor?" / "Your name doesn't ring a bell." / "I'm about to run into a meeting." / "I don't accept solicitation calls." (Trent Dressel — "I'm officially cold calling again!" / "Things I Learned from 53,000 Cold Calls" / "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever")
- Prospect's internal monologue on the open: "Who is Trent? Why is he calling me? I don't have time to talk right now." (Trent Dressel — "The BEST Cold Call Opening Line")
- Skeptical-buyer pushback: "I get calls like this all the time, everyone's got a solution — why should I spend my time on this? What's so special about you that I haven't heard before?" (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play")
- Post-CTA objections: "We don't have budget." / "We're already using [competitor]." / "Now's not the right time." / "We just renewed." (Trent Dressel — "I'm officially cold calling again!")
- Hidden buyer motivation (risk-aversion, not ROI): "I have two kids at home, I work for this big Fortune 500 company, and I just don't want to make too much noise and take a risk that loses the company money." Buyers want to avoid getting fired and avoid extreme risk. (Trent Dressel — "3 Easy Steps to RUIN A Sales Career")
- Why a prospect buys at all: so they can "look better at their company, make more money, save money, mitigate risk." (Trent Dressel — "A Rough Quarter Ahead for Cold Calling")
- The buyer's busy reality: "they have 50 emails to respond to, two proposals to create, someone on their team may have just quit, and they want to get to happy hour early or their kid's soccer game." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever")
- Positive buy-signal: "I'm doing well, how are you?" (= permission to run your talk track). Soft-yes: "Of course that's something I care about." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever")
- Price pressure: "Is this the lowest price you can offer?" (Trent Dressel — "Sell Like a Champ")
- Salesperson's own scarcity self-talk in a down market: "It's really hard to sell into this environment, budget cycles are getting destroyed, sales cycles are taking forever." (Trent Dressel — "Tech Layoffs in 2022")
- VP's brutal teaching rejection: "You failed at Sales 101 — you didn't even tell me what your company did." (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Course offer + risk reversal: paid cold-call course (script + cold email + prospecting + 1-on-1 role-play call), social proof "over 1,000 reps have used it," guarantee "full money-back — message me on LinkedIn if you don't find it helpful." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play")
- "Conquer the Cold Call" CTA: "over 500 reps purchased it — go look at the feedback: more success, higher income, more promotions, more confidence to destroy the phones." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- Guarantee-as-proof claim: "No rep that has ever used this consistently day to day has ever missed quota." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- Free-front-end funnel: free 90-min "Tech Sales intro course" → paid program with coach network, weekly group coaching, mock role-plays, 1-on-1. Proof: "thousands successfully land their sales positions." (Trent Dressel — "10 Sales Job Interview Questions and Answers")
- Low-commitment meeting offer (relationship/renewal play): "I don't expect you to change what you're doing today — I just want 15 minutes to introduce who I am, so when your renewal comes you're fully informed of what's out there." (Trent Dressel — "How to make a cold call in 2024")
- Value-anchored pricing logic: if the problem costs them $100M, charging $10M is justified — frame price against the cost of the problem, not the cost of the product. (Trent Dressel — "3 Easy Steps to RUIN A Sales Career")
- Risk-reversal baked into every meeting ask: "If we both see alignment, we continue — if not, we absolutely can part ways." (Trent Dressel — "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD" / "I Cold Call for a living")

### Objection handling
- **Universal acknowledge-then-reframe formula**: acknowledge the objection → add context / a reason it makes sense to meet → flip it back as a question. "I'm certainly not expecting your team to change, and I'd be surprised if you didn't have something in place. May I ask who your current provider is?" (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play" / "I'm officially cold calling again!")
- **"We already have something in place"**: "I figured you did — by the end of our conversation you'll either feel more confident in your existing provider, or see areas of opportunity worth considering. We're looking to be your partner." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Calling Script Ever [Template]")
- **Incumbent reframe**: "They're fantastic. What we find from customers who switch is they hit limitations with data accuracy, miss integrations they need, and may be paying more than they need to — so while I don't expect you to change, it'd be worth talking through as your team grows." (Trent Dressel — "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play")
- **"No budget" → agree and disarm**: "That's fine, I didn't expect you to have budget. I don't think you'll change anytime soon — but to stay informed of best practices and what's out there, all I'm asking is a 15-minute meeting." (Trent Dressel — "How to make a cold call in 2024")
- **"I'm about to run into a meeting" → call the clock bluff**: "Okay, you've got 11 minutes — so you have some time. Can you give me 30 seconds to tell you why I'm calling?" Never let them rush you; you control the tempo. (Trent Dressel — "Why Cold Calling Is SO HARD")
- **"Send me an email"**: "Happy to — though emails usually aren't the best use of your time. It'd be more valuable to set a quick intro; if there's alignment we continue, if not we part ways." (Trent Dressel — earlier batch echo, reinforced across the cold-call videos)
- **Uncover the REAL objection (the "pizza" reframe)**: "I don't want pizza" → "Why?" → "I'm on a diet" → "We also sell salads" → "Actually I'm not hungry." First objection is usually a brush-off, not the true blocker — keep digging. (Trent Dressel — "Sell Like a Champ")
- **Dig on a stated need**: when they say "our process isn't working," don't fire the next scripted question — ask "Why does it *matter* that your process isn't working?" (Trent Dressel — "Sell Like a Champ")
- **Active-listening mirror**: "To make sure I'm hearing you right, it sounds like you don't have the bandwidth and don't want to meet until [date]." → pivot ("[that date]'s far off — maybe we connect next month instead"). (Trent Dressel — "11 Skills Every SDR Needs To Master")
- **Reframe "no" as timing, not disinterest**: "People telling you no doesn't mean they're not interested — it just means they don't want to buy right now." (Trent Dressel — "11 Skills Every SDR Needs To Master")
- **Pre-write your objection responses**: list your most common objections and write your exact replies — "if you can't write down how you'd respond, you have no chance of responding on the actual phone." (Trent Dressel — "The Ultimate Cold Calling Script")
- **Kill the desperation leak ("quota breath")**: "Frame every interaction so the prospect needs me more than I need them" — be willing to walk. Desperation ("what's your process, who's signing?") leaks and kills deals; abundance + a consultant/partner posture closes. (Trent Dressel — "I'm struggling to perform right now" / "The Best Cold Call Script Ever | Live Role Play")
