- 3 business-development growth plays: Product BD (integrate your product into a bigger partner's — Musixmatch→Spotify), Distribution BD (a platform pushes your product; exclusive vs everywhere), Channel BD (resellers/consultants sell yours for a commission). (Patrick Dang — "Business Development Secrets")
- Control-the-timeline close: challenge a far-off decision date ("why 3 months, not 2 weeks?") → force a yes/no, never a maybe → attach a time-bound incentive that genuinely disappears after the date. (Patrick Dang — "3 Secrets To B2B Sales Success")
- 80/20 rule of selling: talk 20%, listen 80% — the best salespeople are the best listeners, not the best talkers. (Patrick Dang — "Sales Mistakes To Avoid")
- Gatekeeper play: "Can you help me?" — EAs are in their role because they like helping; a strong, relevant reason for the call beats every trick. (John Barrows — "The Cold Call Structure...2026")

### VOC language
- "Let me think about it" / "I might need to talk it over with my boss" — the polite stall that hides the real blocker (no budget, no trust, an approval process). (Patrick Dang — "Sales Objections - Let Me Think About It")
- Price pushback (verbatim): "Eight thousand dollars… I feel your price is too high. I was expecting a price closer to four thousand." (Patrick Dang — "Sales Objections - Your Price Is Too High")
- Negotiation buyer games (verbatim): "they go dark, they mention a competitor, they say 'we actually might do this in-house.'" (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — "Negotiation")
- Cold-call brush-off (verbatim): "I'm not interested. I know [the CEO], so if I decide I need to do something, I'll call him directly." (prospect — 30MPC "I Cold Called a Product...")
- "I don't really have a connection-rate problem" — the "I have no problem" deflection; doesn't mean no problem exists, just that they've only had 30 seconds of context. (30MPC — "I Cold Called a Product...")
- Words prospects quietly recoil from: "problem", "buy", "pitch", "honestly / to be honest", "contract", "trust me", "objection" — each carries a negative or distrust-triggering connotation. (Patrick Dang — "7 Words To Avoid In Sales")
- Pain-discovery probe that opens people up: "How does that make you feel?" — and frustration words to listen for: "held back", "limited", "their potential is capped." (Patrick Dang — "The Psychology of Selling")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- ROI reframe that erases price: "Even if you're paying me more, in the end it's free — because you make more money than you spend with me." (Patrick Dang — "Sales Objections - Your Price Is Too High")
- High-ticket defined: any purchase big enough that a human wants to talk to a human before buying (~$1k+); inbound leads (warm, handed to you) vs outbound leads (you go hunt them). (Patrick Dang — "What Is High Ticket Sales")
- Specific offer beats vague: "I help [specific person] achieve [specific outcome]" — too general and prospects can't see the value (e.g. "I help local gyms get more membership signups"). (Patrick Dang — "How To Start A Consulting Business")
- Time-bound incentive to force a close date: "10% off if you sign by end of month" or "free bonus services if we close by Friday" — and the bonus truly vanishes after, so it costs them nothing to lose but motivates now. (Patrick Dang — "3 Secrets To B2B Sales Success")
- Exclusive-distribution lever: a creator with a real fanbase gets paid a premium to go exclusive because the fans migrate to that one platform (Dave Chappelle / Joe Rogan → single platform). (Patrick Dang — "Business Development Secrets")

### Objection handling
- "Create a cost to everything": never give a concession free — if they ask for a discount, you ask for a longer term/timeline; eventually they stop asking. (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — "Negotiation")
- "Fake walk" on an extreme ask: "I might've screwed up — we're so far off it probably doesn't even make sense for me to go back to my CFO. I just want to confirm you're okay with that." Forces them to step toward you. (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — same)
- "Negotiate like a grandma": once they've gotten a fair discount, switch the bucket — stop cutting price, trade tiny non-price items (billing terms, net-45) until they sense you're tapped out. (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — same)
- Mirror their surprise: if a buyer acts shocked at price, act surprised right back ("whoa, that was way more than I thought too… we're never the cheapest, but never out of the realm"), then put it back on them — do you actually know what this costs, or just asking for a discount? (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — same)
- "He who speaks first loses": give the number, then go completely silent. (Arman Farooq / 30MPC — same)
- Reframe the loaded words: "problem"→"challenge", "buy"→"invest / move forward / take advantage of", "pitch"→"presentation / demonstration", "contract"→"agreement", "any objections?"→"is there anything else you need to see before moving forward?" (Patrick Dang — "7 Words To Avoid In Sales")
- "Let me think about it" → ask what exactly they need to think about, surface the real blocker, then propose a group demo with all decision-makers and state plainly what happens at the end (no mystery, no pressure). (Patrick Dang — "Sales Objections - Let Me Think About It")
- Take responsibility, never blame the prospect: if they "don't get it," your messaging failed — simplify until a fifth-grader understands. (Patrick Dang — "Sales Mistakes To Avoid")
- Pressure is a tell of weak selling: "the more pressure they apply, the worse they are — pressure means the value's too low or the payoff isn't clear. Only sell people what they already want to buy." (Myron Golden — "Million Dollar Business Formula")

- Reversal/anchor on contract length: offer 3 months, let them ask for 12 — "I offer them three months and they ask me for twelve, that's our reversal method." (Jordan Platten — "Sales Techniques To Book An Absurd Amount Of Meetings - With Robb Quinn")
- Market-sophistication takeaway (Schwartz): when everyone's claims sound identical, the only way out is specificity — niche down so you can name an exact, tangible result, and pair a believable offer with enough proof. Proof beats offer: lead with volume of named video testimonials. (Jordan Platten — "Copy This Exact Agency Funnel That Made $2.4M")
- Frame ad spend monthly and quote cost-per-lead up front (£15–£40/lead) so the prospect has done the lead math themselves before they hear the price. Benchmark cost-per-booked-call ~£40 (low) to £250 (high). (Jordan Platten — "Live Critique of SMMA Student Failed Sales Call" / "Copy This Exact Agency Funnel That Made $2.4M")
- AI-service pricing + ROI reframe: charge $2.5K–$5K+/mo — "if you help them get a client worth $20K and they pay you three, it's a great return." Real deals: $3,300→$5,500/mo; $2.3K upfront + $3.9K recurring; $750→$10K/mo. (Patrick Dang — "Type This Into Claude To Make $1,000 This Weekend")
- Permission-based opt-in list: give a free PDF/ebook in exchange for name + email; "you've just given them permission to market to you, so it's not unsolicited." (Mike Locke — "Building an Email Opt-In List")
- Free 14-day trial as a frictionless entry offer; lead-magnet ladder (free skill download / free live training with no replays / free consultation) monetized later via nurture. (Jordan Platten — "Best Email Marketing Automation Software..." / Patrick Dang — "I Asked Claude...")

### Objection handling
- Time objection: "I completely understand time is a scarce asset right now — although technically, if I generate you more clients, I'm actually going to SAVE you time on sales. I only want 15 minutes over the next few days, isn't that fair?" Alt: "When ARE you going to have time to grow the business? If you can't dedicate time now, when will it be important enough?" (Jordan Platten — "How To Master SMMA Objections (Close 3x More Clients)")
- Active empathetic listening to defuse: repeat part of what they said back as a question — "You think your new website could be responsible for your sales decline? Why do you think that is?" (Jordan Platten — "How To Master SMMA Objections (Close 3x More Clients)")
- Severe cold-call rejection: "Hang on a second, before you hang up — I'm not trying to sell you anything right now, just give me 10 seconds, I might be able to change your mind." Then book with a hook: "No obligations — if you like, you can take my ideas and implement them yourself." (Jordan Platten — "Cold Calling SMMA Script That Gets 6 Meetings A Day")
- Email-deflection refusal: "To be honest I find emails a bit of a waste of time — what is it you'd like to see that we can't go through right now?" Then redirect to a 15-min call. First dig: "Before I do, what exactly do you want to see in the email?" (Jordan Platten — "Cold Calling SMMA Script That Gets 6 Meetings A Day" / "Live Cold Call Reviews")
- Willingness to walk (pricing): "Confidence is contagious. There's no cost to the buyer walking, and confidence breeds confidence in your customers — they can sense there's no more to be had." When they claim a competitor is cheaper: "We'd come down based on the levers... but if the price-value equation isn't working out, I wish you the best of luck." (Todd Caponi / 30MPC — "How to Overcome ANY Pricing Objection In Sales")
- "It's too expensive" → challenge the logic against their own goal: "You just told me you want an extra £100k/month, and I'm charging 2% of that — do you not think that's a rational investment?" (Jordan Platten — "The Perfect SMMA Meeting Strategy To Close Clients in 2026")
- "I'm not interested" (cold) → "Of course you're not — you've only known me 20 seconds and haven't heard what I've got. Spend 15 minutes, I'll give you free value, what have you got to lose?" Or down-tone: "So you're not interested in growing your business?" (Jordan Platten — "Cold Calling Masterclass How To Book 10x More Meetings")
- "I need to speak to my partner/wife" → isolate it: "What is it you need to ask them — price or value? If you were the sole decision-maker, would you move forward today? What could they say that would stop you?" Then book the other decision-maker onto the call — never allow secondhand selling. (Jordan Platten — "This Boring AI Agency Sales Strategy Has Made $100M" / "SMMA Student Sales Call Goes WRONG!")
- "We worked with an agency before and got no results" → feel/understand + reframe: "I completely understand how you feel, I feel the same — it's frustrating that other agencies damage our reputation. But what I can show you is XYZ." (Jordan Platten — "Cold Calling Masterclass How To Book 10x More Meetings")
- Quantify the cost of inaction ("quick-fire maths of losses"): 300 leads/mo contacted in 2hrs vs 10-min speed-to-lead doubling conversions × LTV × 3 years, then "Can you really afford not to act today?" AI-anxiety urgency: "If your competitors are using AI to win clients right now, how much business are you already losing?" (Jordan Platten — "Close 36.2% of Agency Sales Calls Using This AI Strategy" / "This Boring AI Agency Sales Strategy")
- Silence after the price IS the objection handling — sit in it. "That silence could simply mean yes." Don't fill it with "are you wary of anything?" — that plants doubt and signals desperation. Never offer to negotiate price unprompted — "it devalues the service and shows desperation." (Jordan Platten — "SMMA Student Closes Their First Client! (Live Footage)" / "SMMA Student Sales Call Goes WRONG!")
- "Can you spend less than $1,000?" → hold your floor: "You can, but the less you spend the bigger the uphill battle — there's less meat on the bone to test creatives, so it takes far longer to see returns. I'd advise against it." (Staying true to your word builds trust.) (Jordan Platten — "SMMA Student Signs His First Client...")
- Reframe a "no" using their own earlier confidence score: "You were just at an 8 — what changed?" A "no" is "a request for more information." (Jordan Platten — "This Boring AI Agency Sales Strategy Has Made $100M")
- "I need to know for sure it'll work before I start" → "You will not know for sure. You have to fail to learn — expect to fail in order to succeed, then pivot once you find traction." (Patrick Dang — "Type This Into Claude To Make $1,000 This Weekend")
- "I have no proof / no testimonials" → "You don't have to show that much proof. Get in front of somebody, sell them, get the money, then build the thing" — one client closed $3,300/mo with only a diagram. (Patrick Dang — "Type This Into Claude To Make $1,000 This Weekend")
- "I'm not good on camera" (creator objection) → "You don't have to be good in front of a camera. Be good at what you do and just turn on a camera while you do it." (Myron Golden — "3 YouTube Million Subscriber Secrets")

- One-X-away banner tagline: "You're one AI audit away from growing your business" (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")

### Frameworks / formulas
- Speed-to-lead stats as a sales argument: leads contacted <1 min = 391% higher conversion; 78% of buyers pick the first responder regardless of price; industry avg response = 42+ hrs (Liam Ottley — "8 AI Sales Automations That Feel Like Cheating")
- Lead-temperature ladder: cold (never heard of you) → warm (engaged/referred/gave email) → hot (buying intent); map every acquisition step to moving people down it (Liam Ottley — "The Proven Content System for Unlimited AI Agency Leads")
- Organic Content Funnel (credit Matt Gray): Awareness (rented audience: YT/IG) → capture into Owned (email/SMS via lead magnet) → Nurture (7 touchpoints, case studies/stories) → CTA to calendar → close (Liam Ottley — "The Proven Content System for Unlimited AI Agency Leads")
- "Rented vs owned audiences": followers can be switched off by the algorithm anytime; convert rented attention into owned email/SMS you control (Liam Ottley — "The Proven Content System for Unlimited AI Agency Leads")
- "Give away the information, sell the implementation" (Hormozi): post full free value/templates; the 99% who won't act were never buyers; sell white-glove setup to the "more money than time" crowd (Liam Ottley — "He Made $12,000 in Four Weeks Selling AI Solutions in FB Groups")
- Paid "AI Audit" instead of free discovery calls — reframes your discovery time as the product: stops tire-kickers, financially qualifies, builds a paid relationship before the big offer, productizes knowhow, ~83% convert to dev project (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- "Introductory call" not "discovery call" — rename + warm up beforehand so they know they must pay to be "discovered"; positions you as authority not free consultant (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- Niche-down-to-scale-up: niching forces world-class delivery; once you've nailed one easy use case it opens bigger custom work ("one led us to the other") (Liam Ottley — "How He Makes $25,000 p/m Selling AI Appointment Setters")
- Warm-launch tactic: "Message 20 first-degree connections" telling them "this is what I'm doing now" — got 18/20 replies (Liam Ottley — "How He Makes $25,000 p/m Selling AI Appointment Setters")
- ACDC model — Attract, Convert, Deliver, Collect; map a business across all four, find problems, own the one slice you're best at (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Niche by OUTCOME not industry — own a process you can run across verticals ("incoming lead → booked appointment"); niche by industry later (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- The ax-head approach — lead with the sharp leading edge (one outcome), not blunt force (everything at once); best clients start with one thing and expand (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- "Document first, automate last" — document → process → prove stable → THEN automate; automating unstable processes breaks things downstream (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Pre-call video flow — apply → book → watch pre-call video (covers system, what we do/don't do, pricing indication, results, explicit invitation to self-disqualify) before the call (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Beachhead-then-grow — small audit/POC, "deliver value very quickly," then expand the relationship (counters skepticism in a maturing market) (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- "Agency as research lab" — run the agency to mine real demand with market data, then build the SaaS the market is already asking for (Liam Ottley — "my entire $100m AI plan")
- "Utility is the hardest part of SaaS" — the build is easy; knowing *what* to build is the moat, and the agency hands you that for free (Liam Ottley — "my entire $100m AI plan")
- Copy-the-aggregator play: pick a niche where info is siloed across Discord/Twitter/forums and search misses it → scrape → index → retrieve; pick a niche with enough $ value to charge (hiking=bad, crypto=good) (Liam Ottley — "This Simple AI Startup Idea Just Raised $5.3M")
- The three buyer questions structuring any deal: "Why do anything?" → "Why you (vs. competition, incl. do-nothing)?" → "Why now?" (a16z — "Go to Market Boot Camp: Field Sales")
- Three-lens account map: Users → User-managers → CXOs — each buys on totally different criteria (feature-function vs. architecture/scale vs. business case/strategy) (a16z — "The Why, How, and When of Sales" / "Field Sales")
- Value framework / "secret sauce": Corporate Objective → Business Strategy → Initiatives → Critical Capabilities → your Solution Set; sell top-down not bottom-up (a16z — "Go to Market Boot Camp: Field Sales")
- As-Is vs. To-Be: articulate current state from discovery, then future state with your solution, backed by use cases from similar customers (a16z — "Go to Market Boot Camp: Field Sales")
- Sales Learning Curve: Initiation → Transition → Execution; repeatable model only in Execution; quota math: past Initiation = reps at 1x loaded cost, Execution = 3x, top orgs ~5x (a16z — "Building a Sales Org: Who, When, How")
- Hire-to-sell test: candidates run a mock sales call as the FIRST step; good reps ask 2 questions, bad reps talk a lot (a16z — "Getting Sales Right")
- Self-imposed firing deadline: pick a date, share it with the rep; if you're still on the fence that day, it's a "no" (a16z — "Getting Sales Right")
- Miller-Heiman buyer roles: economic/user/technical buyers + Coach (only informs) vs. Champion (maneuvers for you) vs. Supporter (just votes) (a16z — "Field Sales")
- "Tech-enabled service" wedge: deliver the outcome by hand first (Pilot did books in QuickBooks day one), watch where it's slow/error-prone, then write software for exactly that (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- Pitch structure: open by acknowledging the market's pain/skepticism FIRST ("go negative"), then position yourself as THE solution to that exact problem — felt more credible than hype (a16z — "The a16z Pitch Room: Sandbox VR")
- Reframe a flat/ugly metric into a strength: a "sad, flat" 8-month revenue graph was actually "100% occupancy for six months straight" (a16z — "The a16z Pitch Room: Sandbox VR")
- "Fun to play AND fun to watch" — build the product so usage generates shareable video; any product that outputs video gets free customer acquisition (a16z — "The a16z Pitch Room: Sandbox VR")
- Pitch by hypothesis: "The hypothesis we proved in our Series A was X; the one we'll prove in this Series B is Y" — each funding stage = a clear claim to validate (Reid Hoffman/Possible — "Reid Hoffman pitches LinkedIn to himself")
- "Brand as your compass": feed brand voice/POV into every automated touchpoint as the constraint that keeps AI content consistent and trustworthy; build a custom GPT loaded with the compass + per-format rules (a16z — "Inside a Billion Dollar Company")
- "Throw paint on the canvas first" — give AI a constrained opinionated first draft so creators escape blank-page paralysis (a16z — "Automating Developer Email with MCP and AI Agents")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Performance-aligned offer w/ strong risk-reversal: cosmetic-clinic AI sales agent $2k–$5k upfront + 25–30% commission, guaranteeing "five figures of incremental sales within the first 7 days" (Liam Ottley — "8 AI Sales Automations That Feel Like Cheating")
- AI-staffing-agency framing: "hire" named AI employees (Grace the SDR, Ava the reactivation specialist); $8,500–$20k upfront + $1,500–$2,000/mo + 100% markup on minutes + commission (Liam Ottley — "8 AI Sales Automations That Feel Like Cheating")
- Pricing receipts bank: real-estate voice agent ~$17k impl (50% upfront) + $1,500/mo; realtor follow-up $2,900 + $497/mo; AI SDR from $5k + $1k/mo for 10k messages; proposal generator €2,000 + €1,500 on completion (Liam Ottley — "8 AI Sales Automations That Feel Like Cheating")
- AI Audit front-end: $1k–$5k paid audit as the proof-maker → converts ~83% to $10k–$20k+ dev projects; "exploration milestones" sold up to $10k just for strategy time (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- Voice-AI reseller economics: ~$2,000 setup + $500–$1,000/mo recurring; per-minute markup (base 18¢ → resell 25¢), billed via Stripe (Liam Ottley — "He Makes $2M/Year Selling Simple Voice AI Shovels")
- White-glove upsell on free templates: $500–$1,000 to set it up for you; small $500–$1k wins become referral bridges to $6,000 retainers (Liam Ottley — "He Made $12,000 in Four Weeks")
- Value-anchoring close question: "how much would you have paid for this?" — frame ROI by hours saved across the team (10 people × 4 focus hrs/day = 2,000+ hrs/mo) so the build lands at five figures (Liam Ottley — "I Transformed an Email Marketing Agency with AI")
- Two client types → two offers: zero-involvement ("just give me the result, how much?") vs. full-control/handover; carry both so you stop turning people away (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Continuity hook: build a new feature (no-show recovery: "20% of your no-shows get rebooked"), prove it on 1–2 clients, then roll out to the whole base as a paid update (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Pre-call price-anchoring: tell them up front "we're not cheap" + give a pricing guide in the pre-call video to filter tire-kickers before the call (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Productized two-tier setup with capped hours: simple prompting setup (~8 hrs) €1,000 vs. complex API-integration (~16 hrs, N8N) €2,000; cap hours or scope goes overboard (Liam Ottley — "The Simplified AI Agency Model")
- Revenue-share kickback terms: give the software partner 10/15/20/25% affiliate fee so they're incentivized to send leads; some don't even want a fee because you grow their MRR (Liam Ottley — "The Simplified AI Agency Model")
- Front-end / back-end split: the setup is the no-brainer front-end; "the real money comes afterwards" via upsells (e.g. a 40-hr N8N workshop = €6,000 net); staff delivery with working students/freelancers for ~80% margin (Liam Ottley — "The Simplified AI Agency Model")
- Bundle individual builds (~$8k and ~$3k each) into ~$20k–$30k packages sold to peers in the niche; free lead-magnet tool to seed future paid SaaS users (Liam Ottley — "my entire $100m AI plan")

- Charge from day one: "It's the clearest signal you're solving a real problem" (Pilot later 10x'd its ASP) (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- Fit/qualify rule-of-thumb: a buyer should spend ~1–1.5% of total expenses on the service; "you shouldn't spend 10% tracking the other 90%"; price-floor disqualifier: "we work best for companies spending at least [X]/mo... below that you probably shouldn't pick us" (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- Sales-team ROI test: "At what price could I sell this WITHOUT a sales team?" — the gap between that and the value reps can communicate is the team's worth (a16z — "Getting Sales Right")
- Keep comp simple: pay reps on 1–3 metrics max; pure pay-for-performance — under-pay for under-performance, over-pay for over-performance (a16z — "The Why, How, and When of Sales")
- Referral engine: a personal email — "if you're happy, we'd love an intro to anyone in your network" — later formalized with a referral leaderboard in investor updates to gamify intros (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- "Better than a perpetual annuity": every SaaS customer is worth more than a perpetual annuity because the install base grows >100% YoY even after churn; don't compare S&M spend to this quarter's revenue — it's an investment in future annuities (a16z — "Why SaaS Revenue is Worth More Than Traditional Software Sales")
- Remove all signup friction: "you sign up, you can send an email in the first minute" (vs. competitors' 2-day manual verification) — frictionless onboarding as the differentiator (a16z — "Automating Developer Email with MCP and AI Agents")

### Objection handling
- "Why pay for a call others give free?" → "Because we want you to prevent expensive missteps and expensive guesswork. We plan first, then you invest" — reframes the paid audit as a saving (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- Fear-stack + protective reframe: "the reason these guys fail at AI 95% of the time is they skip the strategy; if you want to be in the 5%, we do it properly" (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- Financial qualifier as objection-filter: "if they won't put up $1–2k for a good foundation, they're not the client you want… if they don't blink at it, you know they're someone you can work with" (Liam Ottley — "How Two 19-Year-Olds Made $320K in 6 Months")
- "Won't they just do it themselves?" → even when buyers can, they prefer an expert in the loop for the latest/greatest + someone to call; sell done-for-you peace of mind (Liam Ottley — "He Makes $2M/Year Selling Simple Voice AI Shovels")
- Vendor-lock-in objection → make no-code the selling point: "you aren't tied to a specific vendor… you can get other people to maintain it" turns a weakness into trust (Liam Ottley — "He Made $12,000 in Four Weeks")
- Over-promise trap → reset: AI isn't a silver bullet; "we reduce specific task workloads ~80% so you can focus on higher-priority work" — under-promise framing that protects reputation (Liam Ottley — "How He Makes $25,000 p/m")
- Lead-with-outcome-not-AI: "If you lead with AI instead of an outcome, in 2026 you'll get crushed" — owners have tried AI tools, weren't impressed; AI is just delivery (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Demo-vs-production reframe vs. "AI can do everything" hype: "the difference between a demo and something production-ready is chalk and cheese" — sell reliability, not magic (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- Disarm team-disruption / "minimize switching": build into their existing CRM (HubSpot/Salesforce) via an orchestration layer rather than forcing a tech-stack change (Liam Ottley — "This AI Business Is Boring But It Makes $500,000/yr")
- "Why trust your education?" → "no business in their right mind buys how to implement AI from a company that doesn't have solid results themselves" — authority from the agency pre-handles credibility (Liam Ottley — "my entire $100m AI plan")
- "Aren't you just selling to us?" → disarm by admitting it: "I'm not going to tell you I'm not trying to make money — of course I am, as are you," then show incentive alignment (Liam Ottley — "my entire $100m AI plan")
- "Will people get pissed off being called by AI?" named head-on, then answered with a live demo where the bot discloses "yes, I'm an AI assistant if you couldn't tell" and still qualifies + books (Liam Ottley — "Building an AI Sales Bot to Call Leads For Me LIVE")
- "Why should engineers see reps make commissions?" → "We're hiring in sales. If you'd pick up that bag, live that life, and get fired when you miss your number — we'll pay you commission too." (a16z — "The Why, How, and When of Sales")
- "No-commission culture" → adverse selection: cap rep upside and you only attract the worst reps; the million-dollar closer joins the company that pays for performance (a16z — "The Why, How, and When of Sales")
- "Our product is going viral, why do we need sales?" → big orgs have a "rejection organism" (politics, security, standards); bottom-up adoption lands but can't expand to managers/CXOs without sales (a16z — "The Why, How, and When of Sales")
- "Sales will ruin our culture" → reframe sales as teaching/educating the customer so they reach their own conclusion; hire for relationships + shared values (a16z — "Embracing Sales")
- Disqualify the eager-but-wrong-fit buyer: be blunt — "Even though you're willing to buy, you shouldn't, because we won't serve you well." (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- Don't leave founder-led sales too early: hand it off before product/message are nailed and you can't tell whether a loss was the product, the rep, or the message (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- Stop chasing perfect: "the product/deck/collateral gets to perfect by interacting with the real world, not by polishing in your office" (a16z — "Pilot / Waseem Daher")
- On "there's no budget": don't accept it — "of course there's no budget, they've never bought anything like it before"; map your solution to a funded initiative and the budget appears (a16z — "Field Sales")
- Pre-empt the elephant: lead with the market's known weakness ("VR winter is real / 73% churn") so the audience trusts you, then dismantle it (a16z — "The a16z Pitch Room: Sandbox VR")
- Beat the "only works in Asia" objection with proof in the skeptic's own backyard: opening US (Bay Area) locations let investors experience it firsthand (a16z — "The a16z Pitch Room: Sandbox VR")
- Handle AI-quality/trust objection with human-in-the-loop: "if I can review and audit all the actions before they go out, and it's faster... maybe I can trust them more than the humans" (a16z — "How GenAI-Based Software Is Advancing Marketing and Sales")
- Counter "AI will commoditize everything": the defensible moat is brand, high-trust workflows, human relationships, and proprietary data (a16z — "Inside a Billion Dollar Company")

## 2026-06-19 04:33 — harvest batch (40 transcripts)

_All 40 from Joanna Wiebe (Copyhackers) — short-form clips on hooks, conversion copy, freelance positioning, and sales psychology._

### Hooks / headlines / subject lines
- "Are you sleeping in a Petri dish?" beat "Your pillow is filled with bacteria" — concrete visceral image > flat fact statement (Joanna Wiebe — "HOT direct response copy... killer ecommerce email")
- Classic Caples open-loop: "They laughed when I sat down at the piano, but when I started to play..." — works on emotional tension of "what's going on here?" (Joanna Wiebe — "What is a hook? (using John Caples)")
- Yes/no → curiosity rewrite: "Is this cosmetic breakthrough better than Botox?" becomes "What if this cosmetic breakthrough ends Botox?" or "Who wants to be wrinkle-free without shooting Botox into their face?" (don't risk an early "no") (Joanna Wiebe — "Could You Be A Copywriter?")
- "Most marketers get this completely wrong" wins views but kills sales (reader feels attacked); "For marketers who already know the basics" converts (reader feels seen) (Joanna Wiebe — "Why Negativity Gets You Views, Not Sales")
- Believable-claim headline beats bold one: "Over the course of a year, nine in 10 of our clients more than double their conversion rates" outperforms "Double your conversion rate or your money back" — time frame + "9 in 10" + "more than double" disarms skepticism (Joanna Wiebe — "Are You Secretly Killing Your Sales With Your Words?")

### Frameworks / formulas
- DOS — Desire, Obstacle, Solution: open matching their desire, name the obstacle in their way (the "enemy"), introduce solution + link. The obstacle is the magic middle (Joanna Wiebe — "#1 Framework To Write Copy")
- Hook = Action + Bait + Tension, all three must overlap. After writing, ask what's the action / the bait (payoff) / the tension (gap between expected and offered) — whichever you can't answer is where to start (Joanna Wiebe — "The 3 Things Most Hooks Are Lacking That Make Them Fail")
- Payoff-first hook writing: nail the payoff before the hook. Complete "By the end of this you'll know how to ___," then ask "is that payoff specific enough to be surprising?" Bait can't exist without a payoff (Joanna Wiebe — "The #1 Sentence That Will Improve Your Video Hooks")
- Tension test (one-sentence): a hook has real tension only if it fits at the end of that sentence and genuinely sounds surprising (Joanna Wiebe — "The Hook Formula Top 1% Creators Use")
- Super hook = stacks 5 loop types at once: Explanation (why?), Mechanism (how does it work?), Revelation (the hidden thing?), Outcome (then what happened?), Stupidity (why would anyone do that?). Different viewers latch onto different loops (Joanna Wiebe — "Why You Need To Be Using Superhooks in 2026")
- AIDA for cold outreach posts: Attention (quote back their problem + desired result), Interest (results you got for businesses like theirs), Desire (profits/success they'd gain), Action (instant gratification or scarcity) — one writer won $10K in projects with it (Joanna Wiebe — "Use Facebook groups to find clients")
- Live diagnostic-model sell: on the call, draw your framework live (e.g. a triangle — List / Offer / Copy, 9 components) and have THEM mark each red/yellow/green. They self-diagnose, see what to fix, and think "I hope I can afford this person." Self-identified problems build the most trust (Joanna Wiebe — "The #1 Best Way To Sell ANYTHING on a Sales Call")
- Confirm-back close: "You said you have problem A. Feature X addresses problem A, which is good for you because solving A was one of the things you confirmed you wanted." (Joanna Wiebe — "Everything is sales")
- Agitation = an interview you put yourself through: keep asking what the problem really costs them (Joanna Wiebe — "How to Write Compelling Agitation Copy")
- Copywork as training: handwrite proven winning copy (subscribe to great emails, copy them by hand) to build muscle memory before writing original (Joanna Wiebe — "You HAVE TO Copy What Works")
- Content must convert, not befriend: don't fall into the "marketing friend-zone" — every piece should open → qualify → convert to a call, not just hang out (Joanna Wiebe — "Don't fall into the marketing friendzone")
- Branding > first-mover: Starbucks copied Pete's layout/concept and branded it better (third place, app, rewards). "You don't need a better product to win — sometimes just a better brand" (Joanna Wiebe — "How Starbucks Made Billions by Copying")

### VOC language
- The feeling you want a prospect to walk in with: "Gosh, I hope I can afford this person" (Joanna Wiebe — "The #1 Best Way To Sell ANYTHING" / "It is not a red ocean out there")
- Skeptic reaction to over-good claims: "Wait, double? Really?" — too-good numbers trigger disbelief, not desire (Joanna Wiebe — "Are You Secretly Killing Your Sales With Your Words?")
- Self-image-threat reaction: "Wait, are they saying I'm getting it wrong?" → reader feels attacked and bounces (Joanna Wiebe — "Why Negativity Gets You Views, Not Sales")
- Reaction to a great resource: "Why did nobody tell me about this earlier?" (Joanna Wiebe — "The Best Copywriting Book For Beginners")
- What a happy client says after conversions jump 2%→4%: "Can you help us write our email sequence? Can you fix our landing pages?" (Joanna Wiebe — "So, You Want To Be a Copywriter?")
- Memorable-email goal phrased as VOC: prospect lies in bed thinking "what was that pillowcase company Joe mentioned today?" — copy that lives in the imagination after the email is closed (Joanna Wiebe — "HOT direct response copy")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Loss-leader door-opener: a $10–20K homepage rewrite isn't the money (you may lose money on it). Jumping conversions 2%→4% makes the client return within weeks with bigger budgets — sell the first project as proof, not profit (Joanna Wiebe — "So, You Want To Be a Copywriter?")
- High-value retainer play: specialize in ONE channel that needs constant work (email, social selling, AEO/GEO) so you can sell retainers. Clients pay $20K/mo just for email optimization because "good emails sell on repeat" and ROI dwarfs the fee; agency hit $1M in year one (Joanna Wiebe — "How Copywriting Can Make You Rich")
- Guarantee-phrasing risk: "Double your conversion rate or your money back" can read as too-good and trigger skepticism — a softer, believable claim sometimes outperforms a bold guarantee (Joanna Wiebe — "Are You Secretly Killing Your Sales With Your Words?")
- Raise your rates: underpricing signals "copywriters don't deserve money / nobody here has the skills." If you can't confidently raise rates, fix skills, fix confidence, or change to a better audience (Joanna Wiebe — "I'm gonna RANT about underpricing your services")

### Objection handling
- "Won't they know I'm selling?" → "Yeah, you're allowed to sell. You're allowed to assume they're ready." (Joanna Wiebe — "Don't fall into the marketing friendzone")
- Be trusted, not liked: trust comes from understanding the problem better than the person who has it. Stop "agreeing your way to a yes" and lead the conversation like an expert (Joanna Wiebe — "Hard Truth About Sales Conversations")
- Strategic silence: after stating price, hold silence (7 sec feels like an eternity); pause ~3 sec before answering hard questions. Extended silence after an offer raises acceptance ~35% and signals confidence (Joanna Wiebe — "The Secret Skill To Win Any Negotiation")
- Lead with WHO you help, not what you built: Microsoft shifted from "a computer on every desk" (object) to "empower every person... to achieve more" (outcome). Answer "what's in it for me?" and "why should I care?" (Joanna Wiebe — "How To Improve At Sales SUPER Fast")
- Problem-matching before pitching: prove you understand the prospect's specific problem in their exact language first, or the solution "just sounds like noise." Stop pitching, start mirroring (Joanna Wiebe — "Avoid This #1 Sales Mistake")
- Mirror self-identity, don't threaten it: ask "am I reflecting their self-image or threatening it?" — make them think "I see you," not "you're broken" (Joanna Wiebe — "Why Negativity Gets You Views, Not Sales")
- Sell on feeling, not just logic: people decide on how they feel about you; make them feel valued before you ask and they're already leaning yes (Joanna Wiebe — "Sales Secrets of the Top 1%")
- Counter the saturation objection: "It is not a red ocean out there — there's lots of room, and faster ways to build authority than ever" (Joanna Wiebe — "It is not a red ocean out there")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees

Don't turn it, don't discount, don't go back to selling: agree ("yeah, it is expensive… what isn't these days? Anyway, sign here") then re-present the contract. - Reverse-engineer price: start from "what do I want to earn?" ÷ "how many customers?" = price per customer — not "what can I get away with" or competitor averages (Mike Killen — "How Much Does Email Marketing Services Cost?")
- Pricing circle: charge on the NICHE + PROBLEM you solve (center, closest to the customer), never on "who you are" (freelancer) or "what you do" (email marketing) — outer rings, furthest from the customer. "Shift stale warehouse inventory with email" = a 10-grand problem; "10 grand of email support" = unsellable (Mike Killen — "How Much Does Email Marketing Services Cost?")
- Charge for the result, not the deliverable: "Are you delivering 10 grand of email marketing, or 10 grand of RESULTS?" (Mike Killen — "How Much Does Email Marketing Services Cost?")
- Core offer must carry $3,000 of MARGIN (e.g. a $5K product that costs $2K to run); high-ticket = >$10K (aim $2K/mo), recurring = >$1K/mo. The trap: delivering $25K of work for $3-5K (Mike Killen — "EVERY agency should be selling this funnel for $25,000")
- Close-on-the-call mechanics: give ONE price number, then go silent and let them chew; close with "It's a $3,500 deposit, then $2,500/mo for 11 months — we can get started today, is that card payment?" Keep returning to "let me take the $3,500 and we get started today" (Mike Killen — "Close $25K clients EASILY...")
- "Good enough is good enough": an ugly ad to the RIGHT audience beats a beautiful ad to the wrong one (Groupon launched with manual PDF vouchers + PayPal). Don't over-polish before proof (Mike Killen — "This SECRET Google doc blew up my agency sales")
- Don't advertise until consistently $20K/mo; double down on the ONE offer that works instead of diversifying products. Raise price by changing the OFFER (the end result you promise), not the delivery — went $100/mo → $2,000/mo by changing only the promised outcome (Mike Killen — "Copy this and make $10,000 in 30 days")
- Encourage unsubscribes for list hygiene: degrade an "engaged" tag after 30 days no-visit → run win-back emails → auto-unsubscribe dead contacts. - Finish EVERYTHING with a close — finish questions with a close, objections with a close, the pitch with a close. Never end on "does anyone have any questions?" (open-ended = invites the stall) (Mike Killen — "5 mistakes people make when pitching marketing funnel projects")
- Pressure ≠ hard sell. Customers like pressure because it explains why to act now; spell out the literal next step ("sign here, send 50% deposit, we start today") — it may be their first time hiring a pro and they don't know what to do (Mike Killen — "5 mistakes people make when pitching marketing funnel projects")
- Don't pitch your CV/bio up front: "I don't care about you one bit until you show how much you care about MY business." Drop your one-line authority only just before the solution (per Oren Klaff's Pitch Anything) (Mike Killen — "5 mistakes people make when pitching marketing funnel projects")
- Flip-the-frame close: just before closing, ask "what kind of customer are you to work with?" — they start selling themselves to you and chasing the deal (Mike Killen — "5 mistakes people make when pitching marketing funnel projects")
- Decision-maker rule: if they're not the sole decision-maker, stop and rebook with everyone present — "it'd be unfair to expect you to relay a pitch I've practiced for years" (Mike Killen — "Close $25K clients EASILY...")
- Set the pace to control a short call: "I've got calls back-to-back so only ~15 mins — I'll ask a ton of questions and tell you if/how I can help; if I can't, I'll point you elsewhere. Sound okay?" Interrupt context-dumps with "I'll stop you there — I promise we'll get to that" (Mike Killen — "Close $25K clients EASILY...")
- Know when to stop selling: once they say "send the proposal," STOP selling — going back to selling re-opens doubt. Switch to closing (deposit + signature) (Mike Killen — "'Too expensive' isn't an objection")

### Frameworks / formulas
- 7-tip sales-funnel build: (1) think like your prospect (VOC research from calls/communities), (2) break the funnel into mini-goals/outcomes, (3) track each mini-goal, (4) implement with a standardized/repeatable naming system, (5) launch and WAIT (≥100 leads before any change), (6) adapt & adjust the broken step, (7) make it better — never set-and-forget (Greg Hickman — "How To Create A Sales Funnel That Actually Works (7 Tips)")
- Productize-to-$1M 5-step blueprint: Stage 1 Offer positioning → 10k/mo ("I help [ICP] achieve [specific measurable result]" — IHAR avatar/achieve-result framework); Stage 2 Systematize delivery → 30–40k/mo (list every step → group into 3 named phases → make a visual map); Stage 3 Productize DFY into a DWY offer → 50k/mo; Stage 4 Minimum marketing system → 84k/mo (= $1M/yr) (Greg Hickman — "How I Productized My Service to $1M Per Year")
- "Pre-sell, don't build" productization: map your DFY process into a live 6–12 week group, pre-sell it to past clients/email list BEFORE building it, deliver live (Monday training + Thursday Q&A), gather assets as you go = "paid R&D" (Greg Hickman — "How I Productized My Service to $1M Per Year")
- Minimum marketing system: short-form content (reps to nail messaging) → long-form/VSL → capture email → 1–3 value emails/week with a clear CTA to book a call; "go from chasing to attracting, from responding to demand to creating demand" (Greg Hickman — "How I Productized My Service to $1M Per Year")
- Sales-consultation skeleton (time-boxed): set agenda & take the lead (1–3 min) → diagnose with questions (20–25 min) → pitch (90 sec, vague & results-only) → offer/price (1 min) → handle objections (20–25 min); prospect talks 80%, you talk 20% (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- Long-call thesis: run consultations 60–90 min (or 30+60 split) — first 30 = Discovery; longer calls = max price + 7–10yr client retention; "like a doctor diagnosing before prescribing" (Andrew Argue — "Sales Calls Tips for Accounting Firms")
- Close on the first call: no invoice/proposal/engagement letter until they've paid by card — payment is "a logical next step," not a hard sell (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- Value-extraction / dollar-anchor: make the prospect quantify the value themselves ("if you'd had these reports Jan 1, how much more profit could you have made?"); attach a $ figure across money, time, and emotional-anxiety axes (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- "Surround the pain": when you hit a pain point, don't move on — "stab it from different angles" like a dentist pressing the sore tooth until they're in panic mode wanting it fixed (Andrew Argue — "7 Strategies...")
- "Get them naked" diagnostic stack: rapid-fire uncomfortable money questions (how many bank accounts/credit cards, business+personal debt, what you pay yourself, what you set aside for taxes) — the more uncomfortable, the better (Andrew Argue — "7 Strategies...")
- Pre-load objection-handling with stories: tell 4–5 stories on the main objections; for "I already have an accountant," tell of a client with a CPA cousin of 10 years where you found on the FIRST call they'd been overpaying taxes by $X (Andrew Argue — "Handling Objections For Accounting Clients")
- Existing-client upsell ladder: walk them into selling themselves first ("we did a great job on tax prep, didn't we?" → "yes") to reinforce trust, then segue to the next service (Andrew Argue — "7 Strategies...")
- 5-part cold call script: (1) Diffusion, (2) Introduction, (3) Why/reason for the call, (4) Qualification questions, (5) The ask — diffuse on TIME not fake rapport: "I know you're busy so I'll be quick" or "Have I caught you in the middle of something?" (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- Introduction = one sentence: who you are + where from + outcome you deliver — "I'm Jordan, director of [agency], I help restaurants get more clients/month using social media" (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- Gatekeeper script: "Can I speak to [Owner] please?" → if asked why: "I've been helping a restaurant in the local area get more clients... it's not a sales call, don't worry" (light laugh) → if owner's out, ask best call-back time AND their email; rules: never pitch the gatekeeper, don't script your voice, never lie — befriend them (Jordan Platten — "How To Get Past The Gate Keeper")
- 3 reasons people say yes: (1) they desire the product, (2) they can vision the outcome, (3) they trust you — build all three before stating a price (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently")
- Discovery → Tie-in → Present → Close: probing questions so THEY dig up buried problems → tie problems to money/family impact → set a revenue target between current and dream → present and close (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently")
- State the price then GO SILENT — let the prospect speak first; the moment you keep talking you start justifying and shatter the trust (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently" / "How to Perfect Your Sales Process")
- 3 selling weapons: Stories (give them your founding epiphany + a case study of someone in their exact position), Status (lead with value, you only need to be one step ahead to be the expert), Scarcity (limited capacity/FOMO) (Jordan Platten — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone Anytime")
- High-ticket = two-step: anything over ~$1,000, never sell on first contact — use the cold call only to book a meeting, close on the second (Jordan Platten — "How to Perfect Your Sales Process")
- ABC of selling (Daniel Pink): Attunement (take the customer's position), Buoyancy (stay above rejection), Clarity (focus you + the customer on the same thing) (Jordan Platten — "$60,000 Facebook Ads Client Signed")
- Record your own calls for 7–14 days (or have others critique them) — you only hear your own voice live, not what the prospect hears; fastest way to improve delivery (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- Webinar storyline (60-min, sells high-ticket): Setup (who it's for/not) → Agenda (3–5 takeaways) → Bio/authority → Pre-frame (your "aha," old way vs new way) → 3 content blocks → Recap → CTA (application) → FAQ; each block = name the Shift → Old way → New way → cost of not changing vs upside of the shift (Greg Hickman — "Webinars For Closers")
- Eli's 10 Clarities (cover ALL before the offer or the missed one becomes the objection): Pain, Cost of inaction, Desire, Finances, Roadblocks (incl. spouse), Trust, Self-doubt, Timing, Coachability, + they must WANT your help (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- "10 doors" model: every clarity you fail to tie down is an open door the prospect escapes through; lock each so the only path to their goal runs through your offer (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- Leadership-Based Selling 3 rules: (1) your job is the prospect's best interest, (2) that's almost always outside their comfort zone, (3) they'll fight tooth-and-nail to stay in it (Greg Hickman — "Increase Your Sales Potential")
- 9-email playbook (3/week, batch a month in ~half a day): Testimonial, Top-of-funnel promo, Freestyle story, 9-word email, 5/1/30 offer, Two-step "comment X below," Client interview, Straight offer, Game-plan/diagnostic invite (Greg Hickman — "Emails That Get Clients")
- Primary vs Secondary funnel: primary converts the ~15% ready-now; secondary is multi-channel follow-up (email + group + DM) for the 85% who buy later (Dean Jackson "More Cheese Less Whiskers") (Greg Hickman — "Your Secondary Sales Funnel")
- Hire-a-salesperson trigger: consistently 10+ qualified calls/week, then flex your own calendar to 20 for 30 days to prove volume is sustainable, then phase the new rep in 5→8→10 (Greg Hickman — "When to Hire a Sales Person")
- Follow-up math: ~5–12 touches to close; following up turns "100 calls into 400" — most sales aren't made on the first call (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close A Social Media Marketing Client With Cold Calling")
- KPI clarity rule: when running client ads, optimize for ONE number (cost per lead or per conversion) and back-calc the max you can spend per lead from the client's close rate + margins, with a safety margin (Iman Gadzhi — "SMMA Owner Day In The Life VLOG")
- "Influencer arbitrage / audience hijack": partner with micro-creators (20–100k) who can't monetize, build an AI info-offer, take a rev-share cut — present an opportunity, don't sell (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy & Paste THIS Strategy to Make $13k/Month with AI in 2026")
- Validation-before-build stack: check ClickBank gravity scores, scan Facebook Ads Library (advertiser count + how long ads have run = profitability + creative-variation count), sort marketplaces by "most money made" (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy This Method To Make $2,700/Week with Digital Products")
- "Unique value zone" (market → niche → UVC): go a layer deeper until the buyer thinks "this was made just for me" — digital planners → wedding planner → wedding budget tracker for destination weddings (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy This Method To Make $2,700/Week with Digital Products")
- "One step ahead" expertise rule: a level-10 helping a level-8 and a level-3 helping a level-1 are equally valuable; value = solving the problem of someone just behind you (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy This Method To Make $2,700/Week")

### VOC language
- The stall menu prospects use to dodge the close: "I need to talk to my business partner / my spouse," "give me more time to work through my process," "just send me an invoice / engagement letter / your QuickBooks file and we'll go from there" (Andrew Argue — "160 Minutes To Close 1 Paying Client!")
- The seller's own self-sabotage voice at the close: "I'll just send you an invoice... and then we'll go from there" — the comfortable move that kills the yes (Andrew Argue — "160 Minutes To Close 1 Paying Client!")
- Limiting beliefs to dismantle: "I'm an introvert, I'm bad at sales" and "cold calling doesn't work" — excuses people tell themselves to avoid the pain of evolving (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close A Social Media Marketing Client With Cold Calling")
- Creator pain: "they like making content, they don't want to think about monetizing — that's like asking a chef why he doesn't know how to DJ" (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy & Paste THIS Strategy to Make $13k/Month")
- Beginner desire: "most people in 2026 just want to quit their job — they don't care about Rolls-Royces or private jets" (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy & Paste THIS Strategy to Make $13k/Month")
- "The call went great but then they didn't move forward." / "This was my dream client and they didn't buy — why?" (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- "I know I need to show up more, I need to produce content, I just don't know what to say." (Greg Hickman — "Lead Nurture Strategy")
- "Wow, you were so generous with your time that I feel like I don't even need you — I can do it myself." (the over-giving trap) (Greg Hickman — "Increase Your Sales Potential")
- DFY buyer's hidden desire: wants to feel "off the hook," "warm and fuzzy," not own their business — "we got this, you'll have nothing to worry about" (Greg Hickman — "(Leaked Coaching Call) Selling DFY vs DWY")
- Price-stall objections, verbatim: "We can't really afford that right now," "Can I pay you on commission?", "Can I pay at the end of the month?", "Can I give you a percentage of my company?" (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently")
- Restaurant-client pain, verbatim: "We're really struggling on Tuesdays... I think that new competitor down the road is killing our business." (Jordan Platten — "Secret Of Sales")
- "Are you going to burn me too? I want to see your entire operation before we get into this" — distrust from prospects burned by bad agencies (Jordan Platten — "$52,000 A Month SMMA Owner...")
- Manager-tier stall: "Sounds great, but we need to check this out with Bob the owner" — triggers a weak second-hand sale (Jordan Platten — "How To Find Social Media Marketing Clients")
- Agency-vs-hire objection: company "looking to hire a marketing director in-house" — the live decision an agency competes against (Jordan Platten — "$60,000 Facebook Ads Client Signed")
- Buyer-readiness sweet spot as a feeling: not pure "f*** yeah" (not taking it seriously) and not pure fear (not ready) — the buy zone is excited AND a little nervous (Greg Hickman — "How To Know If A Prospect Is Ready")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- First-call close mechanics, stated as routine: "great, let's set up a kickoff — Tuesday at 4? I'll send a calendar invite and request list, and the first payment is $1,500/month — Visa, Mastercard, or Amex?" (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- Quantified value-promise as price justification: "based just on today's conversation, I'll save you at least $17,250 in 2018 and every year forward — probably more" (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- Reject the slow buyer: cut off prospects who won't decide after one (or two) value calls — "if you won't decide after three meetings but expect prospects to decide after one, it won't work"; best clients decide fast, pay up, refer (Andrew Argue — "160 Minutes To Close 1 Paying Client!")
- "I'm looking for 5 people who want [one specific result] in the next 30/60/90 days" — 5/1/30 scarcity+specificity offer, works as email or post (Greg Hickman — "Emails That Get Clients")
- Game-plan/diagnostic offer (email→call): "we look at how you connect, convert, and serve clients, find the bottlenecks, and put together an action plan" — deliver real value, then make the offer on that call (Greg Hickman — "Emails That Get Clients")
- Tesla Method (offer-ladder reframe): sell the most expensive thing first, then strip access/price DOWN to the mass-market product — go down the ladder, not up (Greg Hickman — "Webinars For Closers")
- Application gate: anything over ~$3k or any monthly retainer drives to an application, not a buy button — "I set aside time... go to this URL, answer a couple questions, and you'll speak to someone on our team" (Greg Hickman — "Webinars For Closers")
- Incentivized-referral engine: ask happy clients (after results land) for intros; give £100/mo off retainer per signup; keep pricing confidential so the referred client never learns the referrer's rate (Jordan Platten — "How To Turn Your Clients Into Your Sales Team")
- "Unsuitable" prospect → productized consulting: flat £500 for ~3 hrs DFY (revamp FB page, one-page Shopify, likes campaign, infographic) + a 1-hr teaching call, "you pay ad spend on top," then ongoing per-call consulting (Jordan Platten — "How To Turn An 'Unsuitable Prospect' Into A Consulting Client")
- No free trials, min 1-year contracts — framed as "marketing isn't a short-term play; building a sustainable brand takes a sustainable amount of time"; salesperson comp = 10% recurring on retainers they close (Jordan Platten — "$52,000 A Month SMMA Owner...")
- Action-taker fee waiver (scarcity close): "Our best clients are action takers — decide on this call today and I'll waive the £1,000 upfront setup fee" (Jordan Platten — "How to Sell Anything to Anyone Anytime")
- Never justify your price — banana/TV analogy: justifying a good product makes the buyer suspect something's wrong; "this is my service charge, like it or lump it" (the mindset) (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently")
- Agency-over-in-house pitch (the $60K close), ~10 conversational slides: lead with (1) Cost — no salary/benefits/insurance/taxes/training, (2) Expertise + no vacation gaps, (3) a team beats one hire + "we have a reputation to lose, an employee doesn't, so we get results fast" (Jordan Platten — "$60,000 Facebook Ads Client Signed")
- Rev-share over upfront: with ~100%-margin digital products, hand creators 20–50% of revenue and still keep most — "you only spend money once you make money, zero risk"; keep beginner risk "as little as humanly possible" so you can keep spinning the slot machine (Iman Gadzhi — "Copy & Paste THIS Strategy To Make Your First $1,000 Online")
- Agency retainer ladder: min £4,000/mo up to £12–15k/mo; won't take £15–20k offers outside proven niches — niche-fit > revenue (Iman Gadzhi — "that was a BAD sales call...")
- First $100k can come entirely from "friends, family, network, acquaintances, existing clients" — no cold traffic needed; know your numbers (appointments needed to hit target) (Andrew Argue — "Supercharge Your Sales: Achieve Your $100,000/month Goal with Tax Planning")
- Lead-magnet data tip: collect phone number on the opt-in so you can CALL registrants — "they'll be shocked you're calling... not a lot of people do it" (Greg Hickman — "Lead Nurture Strategy")
- Success guarantee as a referral engine: "we guarantee people's success — that confident in our delivery; our customers become our promoters and we get more referrals than cold clients" (Jordan Platten — "How to Perfect Your Sales Process")

### Objection handling
- Pre-empt, don't rebut: cover all 10 clarities before the offer so objections never surface — "miss the cost of inaction and THAT becomes the objection"; lock the door with their own words: "earlier you said you need this now — did that change?" (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- Cost = cost of inaction, not price: quantify what staying stuck costs monthly, and that it's "not always money" (longer hours, strained marriage) (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- Decision-maker pre-frame: confirm "are you the sole decision maker, or is there anyone else?" before the pitch — if a partner isn't on the call, reschedule (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")
- DFY→DWY reframe: "doing everything for them puts them in handcuffs — would YOU put your business's success entirely in someone else's hands? No. So why let your prospect?" (Greg Hickman — "(Leaked Coaching Call) Selling DFY vs DWY")
- "Disconnect from the sale": go in to lead them to their best decision, not to close — sometimes that means telling them NOT to buy yet (and they come back, often within 90 days) (Greg Hickman — "Increase Your Sales Potential")
- Acknowledge, never block: "you never block an objection — you loop around it. You won't win by telling the other guy he's wrong; acknowledge, add more info, and he's cool" (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close A Social Media Marketing Client With Cold Calling")
- "Objections are just a reflexive shit-test": most early objections aren't real rejection — it's the same reflex as brushing off a stranger on the street before he could offer you a million bucks; hold your character and they settle (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close...")
- "We already have someone in-house" reframe: "perfectly fine — most businesses I call already work with someone. I'm not calling to sell you, just 15 minutes to show how we could make your business better" (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close...")
- Belief precedes objection-handling: "if you don't believe you're offering them a million bucks, you won't push through the objections" — conviction is what survives the shit-tests (Iman Gadzhi — "How To Close...")
- Keep the pitch vague + results-focused: "talk too much about what you're DOING rather than the results and they'll start to doubt you and back away" (Andrew Argue — "How to Master a Sales Consultation")
- Reframe "cost" as "investment" everywhere: a buyer who pays "decided they'd rather have the service than the money," so it's always an investment, never a cost (Andrew Argue — "7 Strategies...")
- Price objection (#1 objection): "My service charge is irrelevant to you. I don't want to make you £1,000, I want to make you multiple thousands... in a couple months you'll wonder why I'm not charging MORE" — reframe fee vs return (Jordan Platten — "How To Overcome Objections In SMMA Meetings")
- Anchor the fee against their own high-ticket item: "you have services up to £30,000 — if we sell just one, that's your whole year's service charge paid for" (Jordan Platten — "How To Overcome Objections In SMMA Meetings")
- "I need to check with my husband/partner/board" → refuse the second-hand sale: "I'd prefer you not second-hand sell the idea — let me book a second meeting with both of you and I'll pitch it again myself" (Jordan Platten — "How To Overcome Objections In SMMA Meetings")
- "I don't have the time" → "When ARE you going to have time to grow? You just said you want to expand. Not now? Fine — tomorrow? Next week?" (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- "I'm not interested" → "I presume you're making a lot from Facebook already? No? Then why wouldn't you be interested in making more from a new source?" (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- Universal closer on every objection: "I just want to share some ideas for 10–15 minutes over the next couple days — what have you got to lose?" (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- "So I can see whether we're a good fit for each other" — flips the frame so the prospect qualifies themselves to YOU (Jordan Platten — "How to Write a Cold Call Script")
- Refuse to discount with conviction: "No — what I'm giving you is extremely valuable; people get five-fold ROI within weeks, it's cheap as it is" (Jordan Platten — "How To Close Marketing Clients Confidently")
- Gatekeeper "they're not in" → never end the call: ask the best call-back time AND the email — the email usually reveals the owner's name to use next time (Jordan Platten — "How To Get Past The Gate Keeper")
- Sell-the-meeting when fit is unknown: on a warm/inbound call where viability is unclear, close only the next meeting where you can assess whether you can get results (Iman Gadzhi — "that was a BAD sales call...")
- "Friendly + cooperative" as a disqualifier: if they're difficult/closed-off on the call, that's how they'll be as a client — don't enroll them (Greg Hickman — "How To Handle Sales Objections")

### Frameworks / formulas
- 7-figure VSL sequence: Pain (bold filtering question) → Transformation/Claim (one sentence) → ... each box earns the next; you WANT a big early drop-off so only your 1-3% avatar stays (Ravi Abuvala — "How to write 7-figure video sales letters")
- "Corner store test" for your one-line claim: say it so plainly a shop clerk gets it — "I help people lose 40 lbs in 12 weeks, guaranteed." Kill jargon like "increase your structure." (Ravi Abuvala — "How to write 7-figure VSLs")
- 5 levels of awareness (Schwartz): unaware → problem → solution → product → most aware; ~98% of any market sits in the first three, so leading with "buy my thing" falls on deaf ears (Ravi Abuvala — "Why Your Content Isn't Making Sales")
- "Sale before the sale" 80/20: marketing should do ~80% of the convincing (content, proof, emails) BEFORE the call; sales only handles final objections, sets expectations, closes (Ravi Abuvala — "14 minutes of sales training")
- Google 7-11-4 rule: ~7 hours of content, 11 touchpoints, 4 locations to turn a stranger into a buyer — the spine of the "trust recession" argument (Ravi Abuvala — multiple)
- Zero Moment of Truth (ZMOT): a private research stage now happens BEFORE the prospect ever books or contacts you — win it with pre-call content (Ravi Abuvala — "What We Learned After Analyzing 16,000+ Sales Calls")
- Hybrid offer = best of Done-For-You (high perceived value, near-guaranteed results) + Done-With-You (simple, community) + DIY (scalable, 95% margin) fused into one offer; no offer he's seen scale past $10M lacks this (Ravi Abuvala — "How I Created A Hybrid Offer")
- 3-part pre-call system for 50%+ close rate: (1) strategic qualifying questions, (2) "transfer of trust" video, (3) organic retargeting content (Ravi Abuvala — "The 3-Part Pre-Call System")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Cold-friendly risk-reversal that lifts you above everyone: "you only pay if you have show-up appointments," "you only pay when you close a deal," "we guarantee 30 bookings / 5 clients a month." (Ravi Abuvala — "GRAB Attention with Email Marketing")
- Offer specificity + de-risking stack: "We've helped 378 businesses just like you get the loan in 30 days or less, under 7% interest, with no collateral or income verification." (Ravi Abuvala — "ChatGPT Prompts For A $10M Cold Email")
- Hybrid-offer margin logic: DFY = high perceived value but thin margin/high complexity; DIY = 95%+ margin but commoditized — fuse them to keep value high AND margin high (Ravi Abuvala — "How I Created A Hybrid Offer")
- Tier by qualification, don't bend the core offer: built a cheaper, less-1:1 offer for the $1-10k/mo segment instead of discounting the flagship for unqualified buyers (Ravi Abuvala — "The 3-Part Pre-Call System")
- Honest on-track-earnings in a hiring "offer": post a realistic OTE ($120k) + "minimum 40% close rate on qualified inbound" — inflated numbers attract the wrong closers; "you can't afford top 1%? hire top 5-10% — 80% done beats you doing it all" (Ravi Abuvala — "How To Hire 1% Closers")

### Objection handling
- "It's too expensive" → "Is this a value problem or a money problem?" isolates the real issue before you negotiate (Jordan Platten — "Overcoming Sales Objections")
- "I'm not interested" → don't fold; push back with a like-for-like proof: "Are you not interested in increasing revenue? We're getting Bill's Gym 8x ROI — why wouldn't you want that?" (Jordan Platten — "Overcoming Sales Objections")
- "I can get it cheaper elsewhere" → "Do you buy everything in life on price or on value? You can't pay Kia prices for a Ferrari." (Jordan Platten — "Overcoming Sales Objections")
- Competitor objection → never say "here's how we're different" (you lose the frame); probe the benefit they want, then: "You told me X is your #1 problem — this is exactly how we solve it. Why search anywhere else?" (Ravi Abuvala — "How I Handle Sales Objections")
- "I need to talk to my spouse" ≈ smokescreen for "I'm scared / I want more time"; loop back, surface the real limiting belief, and handle it on the call (Ravi Abuvala — "How I Handle Sales Objections" + "$30M Sales Calls")
- Pre-empt the decision-maker objection early: "Besides you, who else needs to be comfortable with this if we decide it's the right move?" then tie it back if they later stall (Ravi Abuvala — "We Analyzed $30M In Sales Calls")
- Build trust by disqualifying: openly state who you DON'T help and past clients who failed — it makes the right buyer feel "this IS for me" (Ravi Abuvala — "7 B2B Sales Tips")
- Urgency without sleaze: skip fake "say yes now or never"; quantify the money lost by staying the same and what their future looks like if nothing changes (Ravi Abuvala — "7 B2B Sales Tips")
- Never let a prospect leave on "just send me more info" — it hides the real objection; handle it then and there and set crystal-clear next steps (3-5 specific steps) (Ravi Abuvala — "7 B2B Sales Tips")

- Ad-stated guarantee/transformation: "We will build an entire done-for-you client acquisition system and install it in your business in the next three days or your money back." (Ravi Abuvala — "Copy Our $10M Facebook Ad Formula")
- Cold-call risk reversal: "We guarantee we'll get you results in [time] or I'll give you your money back plus a thousand dollars on top of it." (Ravi Abuvala — "Making Money Online in 2024")
- Hiring offer with placement guarantee: "We find, interview, and place a client success manager in the next four days, guaranteed to stay 90 days or you don't pay." (Ravi Abuvala — "Cold Email Marketing Mistakes...")
- Lending offer architecture: "I can get you up to $350,000 at lower than 6% interest in the next 30 days... no income verification needed, even if you're getting denied by the banks." (Ravi Abuvala — "Cold Email Marketing Mistakes...")
- **Product-suite pricing logic:** front-end at impulse range ($7–$35), then make every order bump/OTO as high as possible ($97–$197+); even 10% buying a $197 OTO ~3×'s a $7 front end. Don't give everything away on the $7. (Ravi Abuvala — "I've Built 2,000 Funnels...")
- **Show-up bonus:** offering a bonus for *showing up* (not just booking) the implementation call lifted booking 50%→60%; lock the bonus inside the product "only for those who show up." (Ravi Abuvala — "I've Built 2,000 Funnels...")
- Financing as a conversion lever on checkout: "You can get started for as low as $153/month." (Ravi Abuvala — "I've Built 2,000 Funnels...")
- Stacked guarantee: "We guarantee you'll get your results or we give you your money back AND write you a check for $10,000." Principle: "if you're not afraid of the guarantee, it's probably not strong enough." (Ravi Abuvala — "How To Cold Email...")
- Core risk-reversal: "We will build you an end-to-end marketing system guaranteed to be profitable within 90 days, or your money back." (Ravi Abuvala — "Email Marketing Full Course")
- Scarcity (real, not fake timers): "We're only able to take on two website-design clients per month and we already have one — do you want to get going?" (Ravi Abuvala — "Upselling and Cross Selling")
- **Whoever can spend the most to acquire a customer wins:** add 2–3 upsells + one recurring offer so LTV (~$100) far exceeds a single core sale ($20), letting you outbid competitors on ad spend. Never let the upsell out-shine the original purchase. (Ravi Abuvala — "Upselling and Cross Selling")
- Pay reps on cash collected (after the bad-fit drop-off point), claw back commission on refunds — so they only close the right clients. (Ravi Abuvala — "Why Sales Reps Will Ruin Your Business")
- Hard ICP cutoff: redirect anyone below $50k/mo to YouTube via a jotform gate; DFY priced 30k PIF / 36k over 6 months with a 32% backend crossover. (Ravi Abuvala — "You're Wasting Your Time Selling Coaching")
- **Free-value-first demo as lead-gen:** Camtasia screen-capture critiquing a prospect's own website, sent cold — "here's what you can fix to make more money right now; want more, call me." Landed a $1k consult, then repeated. (Ed Mylett — "How to Get ATTENTION..." — Billy Gene)
- **Proof-led pitch video:** "Here's how I sold $150,000 of wetsuits with Facebook ads on a $6,000 budget. Want to see how? Click here" → 10-min how-it-was-done → "Want me to do the same for your business? Schedule a time." Result: $10k next day. (Ed Mylett — "How to Get ATTENTION..." — Billy Gene)

### Objection handling
- **Call out the elephant:** "I know you get millions of emails like this, people promising the same thing — but here's why I'm different." Saying what's in their head builds trust. (Ravi Abuvala — "Copywriting Tutorial For Beginners")
- **Name the competitor first:** "Most people I know have worked with Zillow.com and had X experience — this is why we're different than Zillow." Pre-empt the comparison they're already making. (Ravi Abuvala — "Copywriting Tutorial For Beginners")
- **"Not enough social proof" reframe:** go deep on the one strong case you have; if you have none, go get a client result first. (Ravi Abuvala — "Cold Email Marketing... Made Me $10M")
- **Money/urgency tie-down close:** "You've been doing this six months on your own and it hasn't worked. We identified you're losing $50k/month. I'm asking for a fraction of that — how much longer are you going to keep losing $50k a month?" (Ravi Abuvala — "Stop Doing Two-Call Closes")
- **Objections are caused by the salesperson, not the prospect** — they come from failing to build enough pain/gap and urgency. No pain = no urgency to buy. Don't lead with external enthusiasm (it triggers fight-or-flight). (Ravi Abuvala — "The #1 Salesman In The World (Jeremy Miner)")
- **Reframe the power dynamic:** "The prospect has the problems, not you. You have the solution — act like it. Why are you qualifying to them?" (Ravi Abuvala — "The #1 Salesman In The World (Jeremy Miner)")
- **Replace weak open-ended closers** ("Would you be interested in exploring this further?") with a concrete CTA — booking link / "leave your number." (Ravi Abuvala — "$10M+ CEO: I actually opened...")
- **Sharpen the qualifying question to filter to the unhappy buyer:** not "Do you use Facebook lead forms?" but "Are you currently happy with the integration between your Facebook lead forms and your CRM?" — a "no" = 10× higher switching intent. (Ravi Abuvala — "$10M+ CEO: I actually opened...")
- **Price objection reframe:** when prospects say "too expensive," check whether they're even qualified before lowering price — most "I'm bad at sales" problems are "I'm selling to people who can't buy." (Ravi Abuvala — "My Sales Team Closes 40%+")
- **"I need to talk to my spouse" — prevent it before the call:** state "all financial decision makers required on this call" in marketing, on the application (only answer = "yes"), and in the confirmation text/email; if they can't confirm, cancel and rebook. (Ravi Abuvala — "How We Close $50,000 Deals...")
- **"I can't make that bold claim":** then make your offer better / add a guarantee — a vague "I can help you" gets no replies; "we guarantee we'll double your business without spending more money" does. (Ravi Abuvala — "How To Cold Email...")
- **No-show / low-intent objection:** people who reply "yes" to the confirmation show at ~95% (vs 40–50%) and close higher; the further out they book, the lower the show rate. (Ravi Abuvala — "The ONLY Sales Page...")
- **Pre-handle objections with content:** keep a library of dedicated objection-handling videos — "some of our other clients had that same objection, here's a video." One recording answers every prospect. (Ravi Abuvala — "My Sales Team Closes 40%+")
- **Sunk-cost reframe (status purchases):** "I was justifying why I still needed the car because I'd already bought it — but I didn't need it at all." (Ravi Abuvala — "Why I'm Selling My Porsche 911")
- **Against "win-win" / "fair" manipulation:** name it. "I want you treated fairly at all times, so anytime you sense I'm not, let's go back to it." Forces criteria onto a vague word. (Ed Mylett — "This ONE Tweak..." — Chris Voss)
- **When attacked/insulted in a negotiation,** don't counter-attack — "You must have a great reason for feeling/saying that. What is it?" Buys thinking time, de-escalates, extracts information. (Ed Mylett — "This ONE Tweak..." — Chris Voss)
- **"That's true for them, not for my business":** "You can't name a business where this doesn't apply — stop resisting the change. The competition will adapt and you'll lose." (Ed Mylett — "How to Get ATTENTION..." — Billy Gene)
- **"I'm not in sales" reframe:** "Yes, you are. Everything in life is communication, and almost everything is negotiation." (Ed Mylett — "Jordan Belfort..." / "This ONE Tweak...")
- **"I'm not entertaining/charismatic":** "You don't have a strength yet — you find it by experimenting. Go take a local improv class for $15." Plus props/music/environment grab attention even if you're "boring." (Ed Mylett — "How to Get ATTENTION..." — Billy Gene)
- **Buyer who wants the result but won't do the work:** surface the incongruence — "champagne vision, beer work ethic, it ain't going to work out." (Ed Mylett — "Jordan Belfort Reveals the Truth..." — Belfort)
