### Frameworks / formulas
- The "111 Strategy": find one person with one problem and give them one result, then scale (Pat Flynn — "Stop selling info and do this instead")
- Three implementation models to sell instead of information: (1) Do it FOR them (service), (2) Do it WITH them (coaching/consulting w/ accountability), (3) Do it with OTHERS (community/cohorts) (Pat Flynn — "Stop selling info and do this instead")
- Validate before you build: test book/product topics through blog posts → email lead magnets → full courses; a lead magnet that earns the email signal proves demand (Pat Flynn — "How to Write a Bestselling Book")
- Launch-event (Tesla) strategy: set a date for the unveiling → hint at details without revealing everything → create content around it pre-launch → involve networks/influencers to amplify → hype + word-of-mouth (Pat Flynn — "Copy This Tesla Marketing Strategy"); funded a $100K Kickstarter in 11h26m off 1+ year of pre-launch hype
- Segmentation lift: split audience into buckets (min leads vs customers; better, 3+ by pain point); open rates 20%→65%, CTR 3.5%→8.5% (Pat Flynn — "Segmentation and Triggers in Email Marketing #6")
- Self-segmentation email: ask "What's your biggest challenge related to [topic]?" → group replies into buckets → link-triggers auto-tag the clicker and drop them into a bucket-specific sequence (Pat Flynn — "Segmentation and Triggers in Email Marketing #6" / "Inside Email Marketing")
- "Email value premise": people don't want more emails, they want the RESULT the email promises — make the lead magnet deliver the transformation FASTER, shorter = more valuable (Pat Flynn — "Email Marketing in 2022 Workshop")
- Autoresponder/welcome sequence: immediate welcome/intro → educational (≈7 days) → educational (≈7 days) → soft intro to product → soft pitch; space education between asks to avoid aggressive selling (Pat Flynn — "How to Setup a Winning Autoresponder Series #4")
- PAS (Pain-Agitate-Solution): Pain (tripods are clunky) → Agitate (wastes luggage space, amateur video) → Solution (the product) (Pat Flynn — "A.I. Robots Can Write Good Sales Copy? Let's Test It")
- Two-step opt-in: button first (creates focus/decision) → form appears on click; removes distractions and lifts conversion (Pat Flynn — "5 Strategies to Get More Email Subscribers #3")
- Content upgrades: post/episode-specific downloadables (not one site-wide magnet) convert far better (Pat Flynn — "5 Strategies to Get More Email Subscribers #3")
- The Soft Pitch Pipeline: (1) build relationship, (2) choose the right product, (3) share your own experience, (4) show proof, (5) THEN pitch — done right, the pitch is nearly invisible (Pat Flynn — "Affiliate Marketing for Beginners (The Soft Pitch Pipeline)")
- Three-tier pricing: base (1X), middle (2X with more bonuses), premium (4-5X with everything) drives buyers to the top tier; food-themed tier names ("Combo Meal", "All You Can Eat Buffet") make premium feel abundant (Pat Flynn — "Niche Site Sales Page and The New LeadPages Marketplace!")
- Launch email sequence: (1) story-based narrative, (2) FAQ/benefits, (3) final-day urgency, (4) last-call reminder; save the most aggressive promo for the final 24h (Pat Flynn — "Making Money While on Vacation?")
- Hook-Story-Offer: every page, email, and ad needs a hook (grab attention), a story (build trust), and an offer (irresistible deal) (Russell Brunson, Young and Profiting — "The Funnel Framework That Skyrockets Course Sales")
- Sales Ladder / micro-commitments: stack small yeses (download, quiz, signup) that build momentum and self-image as an "action taker" until the big ask feels natural (Cialdini consistency principle) (Young and Profiting — "The Funnel Framework That Skyrockets Course Sales")
- Launch-team strategy: a 500-person early-access group reviews, leaves reviews, and shares at launch = built-in social-proof engine; for the book, 40 of 50 targeted podcasts said yes (Pat Flynn — "Lessons Learned from a Best Selling Self-Published Author – SPI TV Ep. 55")

- Handle price/time objections 6-9 times in different contexts across site, social, webinar, and sales page, then focus heavily on the BELIEF objection ("I don't think I can do this") (Jason Fladlien, Young and Profiting — "The Funnel Framework That Skyrockets Course Sales")

- "You don't need hundreds of thousands, definitely not millions, of people looking at you." / "We built a multi-million dollar business before Instagram even hit 50,000 followers." — followers ≠ revenue (Young and Profiting — "Adam Schafer: The #1 Organic Sales Strategy...")
- "Hey [Name]," subject lines outperform formal ones; no-subject or "appropriate person?" subjects lift reply rates because people want to feel helpful/important (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary: NEW Sales Strategies | Part 2")
- "Win + mutual/peer validation = interest straight away" — pair a benefit with social proof in the opener to beat conditioned cynicism (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 1]")

### Frameworks / formulas
- Elevator-pitch formula: "You know how [one avatar] struggles with [one problem]... I help them [one result]." One avatar, one problem, one result — and it's a conversation, wait for their "yeah" (The Futur — "Win More Clients With This Simple Pitch Hack")
- Add an adjective to the avatar ("creative high school students," not "students") and name the negative emotion ("lost and directionless") so the problem lands (The Futur — "Win More Clients With This Simple Pitch Hack")
- Make a story repeatable: tell only the part that's "memorable, different, and unique" so people can retell it when you're not in the room (The Futur — "Is Your Business Pitch Kid Proof?!?")
- Make a stat stick by making it visual + relatable: "half of all plastic goes to packaging" becomes "the equivalent of three Empire State Buildings" (The Futur — "Is Your Business Pitch Kid Proof?!?")
- The $6,500 sales script in order: (1) post proof consistently, (2) artificial scarcity ("3 open slots"), (3) "are you serious?" commitment, (4) lead magnet + simple CTA, (5) compliment + light profiling, (6) ask WHY the goal matters, (7) make them rate it 1–10, (8) ask "why isn't your score lower?", (9) handle pre-known objections, (10) get commitment, then ask for the card (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script (FREE)")
- "Why isn't your score lower?" — the trap question: after they rate desire 1–10, asking why it's not LOWER makes the prospect sell themselves to you (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script (FREE)" / "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- Quantify the unquantifiable: anything (brand value, fitness, identity) goes on a 1–10 scale — "you're just not creative" if you say you can't measure it (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script (FREE)")
- Discovery-question stack: "Where are you in your business? What do you need help with? What have you tried and failed? Who has wronged you? What outcome would you like?" → marry their want to your solution (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- Price emerges from the conversation: (1) establish desired future state, (2) where they are now, (3) what's in the way, (4) confirm "if you got this result it'd be worth $X" (get a yes), (5) "if the solution cost a fraction of that value, would you be excited to move forward?" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- 80/20 talk-time: in the first 80% of the call you talk ~20% (ask, then shut up); flip to ~80% only at the end to connect the dots and prove you listened (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition with Sales Strategies That WORK")
- "May I have your permission to set the agenda for this call?" — earns the right to lead and redirect tangents without friction (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition with Sales Strategies That WORK")
- The fishing close: don't grab the net (price/packages) until the fish points its face at the boat — i.e. until they ask "how do we start, what does it cost?" Then don't go past the sale (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition with Sales Strategies That WORK")
- Inner-frame / outcome-detachment: "stop caring about outcomes, care about the quality of person you are"; desperation makes you less sharp and repels the buyer (the dating analogy) (The Futur — "Sales and Marketing Secrets... John Driscoll")
- Assume everything the prospect says is untrue (not lying — unconsidered): ask "what evidence do you have that's true?" to test their logic as their advocate (The Futur — "How To Say Your Price - Sales Roleplay")
- Identify your avatar by frequency, not demographics (7 Frequencies: Motivator, Challenger, Commander, Healer, Professor, Seer, Maven) — speak in the one they can best HEAR (The Futur — "...Erwin McManus Teaches How To Identify Your Avatar")
- SALES as a process, not a pitch: Serve, Ask, Listen, Empathize, Summarize (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy" / "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Sales = change management: Current State → Obstacle → Desired Future State; the only two questions are "What do they want?" and "What's getting in their way?" (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy: The Kind Way to Sell")
- The 2 Bs: Baseline (current state) and Benchmark (desired future state) — establish both before any performance deal (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- LTV = gross revenue ÷ total customers; Net LTV = LTV × net margin (net is what matters); use "Olympic scoring" (drop top 2 + bottom 2) so outliers don't skew it (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- Cost-Per-Acquisition rule: as long as it costs less to acquire a customer than your net margin, do that deal all day (the "$45-in, $50-out ATM" that scales infinitely) (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- ICE discovery: Impact (on their business) → Challenge (what's in the way) → End goal (the outcome they want) (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- Coaching Habit ladder (Bungay Stanier): "What's on your mind?" → "And what else?" (repeat) → "What's the real challenge here for you?"; be slower to give advice (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course" / "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- Open-question rule: best questions start with "what" (neutral); "how" rushes to tactics; "why" sounds accusatory if your tone is off (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- The 3 listening questions on every call: What did you HEAR (facts)? → What does it MEAN (main point)? → What is the person FEELING? Plus 3 layers: the words → the tone → what isn't said (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- "I noticed..." technique: state the observation, never the label — "I noticed you paused, can I ask what's going on?" not "I see you're uncomfortable" (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- "Suitcase words": any vague word a client uses ("strange," "weird," "interesting") hides a meaning; ask anyway, and use their exact word back, never swap it (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- Retreat and Follow (Blair Enns): raise the objection first, "try to kill the opportunity" and back up; if they're interested they follow. "If you whisper, they lean in; if you shout, you push people away" (The Futur — "...3 Most Common Client Objections" / "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Judo, not karate: don't charge the objection; acknowledge/own it, validate them, use their momentum, then pivot and throw — exploit the hole in their logic (The Futur — "How To Respond To The 3 Most Common Client Objections in Sales")
- Three pricing models, pick by fit: time-based (only when scope is unknowable), project/fixed-fee, value-based (% of value created); hybrid "design-build" = fixed for finite scope + variable for undefined scope (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- Anchoring by relative scale: price the small item ($50–60k logo) against the full ecosystem ($250–400k of touch points); whoever names the number first sets the frame (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work" / "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Price bracketing / sonar: float big round numbers as a range ("could be 10k, could be 50, could be 200") and read the reaction to locate their budget (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Proposal delivery, worst-to-best: (1) email PDF and wait — worst; (2) record a Loom so it carries your voice; (3) BEST — present live, record THAT call, send the recording, book the next meeting before hanging up (The Futur — "What Designers Do to Close $10K+ clients... | Ep. 346")
- Drip the price across the proposal: put each element's cost on its own page as you build value, so the buyer trusts where every dollar goes (vs. "everything, BANG, final price") (The Futur — "What Designers Do to Close $10K+ clients... | Ep. 346")
- Win/loss review loop: export 2 years of closed-lost and closed-won into an LLM, ask "why do I lose?" and "who do I win with?", lean into that ICP; run quarterly (The Futur — "What Designers Do to Close $10K+ clients... | Ep. 346")
- Create the customer (Drucker): keep the product the same, move it to a new buyer category, agitate a problem they already feel, use their language (cell phones → "privacy"/burner phones) (The Futur — "The Scene Every Salesman Needs to See")
- The if/then close: "If you saw a solution that did X, Y, Z, in this time, for this money — would you move forward?", then wait for an EMPHATIC yes, then lock the next step (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy: The Kind Way to Sell")
- The Clarity Call (4-part first-call framework, 15–20 min): (1) Control the frame; (2) Identify the Gap (where they are vs. want to be — bigger gap = more value); (3) Test the time frame ("1–10, how important is fixing this in the next 30–60 days?"); (4) Guide the next step (The Futur — "What Top Sales Experts Know About Client Perception")
- Qualify on buying POWER, not budget: budgets are set by finance for where they ARE; ask about turnover, average deal value, capital created if the problem is fixed (The Futur — "What Top Sales Experts Know About Client Perception")
- "You don't sell IN your content, you sell THROUGH your content." Spammed CTAs read as desperate; demonstrate expertise so they come to you, then route via a clean profile (The Futur — "How to Sell Through Your Content in 2026")
- Profile-as-conversion-asset (LinkedIn): (1) real close-up headshot; (2) banner = free ad space for credentials/proof; (3) description = clear "I do X for Y + benefit"; (4) Featured = your offers with links + thumbnails, not posts (The Futur — "How to Sell Through Your Content in 2026")
- The scarcity-staging loop: pre-announce a specific limited offer → get the market to raise hands → move them to a VISIBLE staging area (they see each other competing) → set ticket date with a 24-hr private window → never raise capacity (The Futur — "Generate Demand...")
- Name-it-to-own-it: distill an idea, give it a unique name (e.g. "Retina Display"); naming it makes you the owner even if the idea isn't new (The Futur — "Generate Demand...")
- "1-1-1 product": One narrow problem, one solution (teach only ONE way), created in one sitting (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- "80% of what makes a webinar work is the offer" — a killer offer lets a mediocre presenter win (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Two-agenda intro + tie-down: "I have two goals — show you how to do X, and sell you something. If I DON'T deliver the first, never buy from me. If I DO, you should feel obligated. Fair?" — gets a verbal yes up front (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Storyboarded testimonial: split ONE testimonial across the pitch — tease in intro, expand mid-content, reveal finale at the offer — so one person reads as three (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Hero Story / Epiphany Bridge (6 beats): relatable start → struggles → aha moment → the new method → proof → service to others (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- Big Promise formula: specific & measurable + ease/simplicity + unique approach + objection handled up front + end-benefit not process + speed/shortcut (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge..." / "Why No One's Buying From You")
- Content filters: run finished copy through 4 filters — cut anything triggering FEAR or CONFUSION, add SAFETY and ENTHUSIASM ("a confused mind never buys, a scared mind never buys") (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- Offer Stack close: core product → break down each component → list bonuses with dollar values → tally total → reveal far lower price → add urgency/scarcity (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- Hook–Story–Offer across all funnel stages; TOFU/MOFU/BOFU: top = capture email with free value; middle = build trust via education + objection handling; bottom = make the decision easy with proof + incentive (Young and Profiting — "Why No One's Buying From You")
- Bottoms-up / driver-tree sales math: work backward from revenue goal to volume of actions (clicks, calls, attendees); separate driver metrics (actions) from result metrics (conversions) (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")
- Collapse time in messaging: "It took me 5 years to master LinkedIn — in my 2-day masterclass you get all 5 years in 2 days" (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")
- The CARE engine: Consistency (show up daily), Abundance (4–5x/week), Relevancy (only what you're known for), Engagement (the conversion happens in comments/replies, not the post) (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 1]")
- The warming process: position via content/social proof first so the prospect says "I've seen you around" — you're halfway closed before you pitch; 6–8 touch points on average before a cold prospect closes (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 1 & 2]")
- ICP + Buyer Persona: derive your Ideal Customer Profile from your last 50 customers, name the actual decision-maker, re-evaluate quarterly; run one-to-few + one-to-many in parallel (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary | Part 2")
- Discovery → Demo → Pricing (don't quote until discovery is done); Wedge strategy: enter with the one product solving their most urgent pain, expand wallet share later (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary | Part 2")
- The Favorite vs. the Fool: when a prospect contacts you their mind is ~70% made up; your job is diagnosing fast whether you're the favorite (~80%+) or the fool (~20%), not "presenting" (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- "That's right" vs. "you're right": "that's right" = they feel understood; "you're right" = they're dismissing you; earn a "that's right" before pitching ("Before I give my perspective, here's what I think YOURS is...") (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- The three voices: late-night FM DJ (calming — use this), analyst (direct, lands like a brick), commentator (warm); never the assertive voice when you want cooperation (Young and Profiting — "Learn How to NEGOTIATE Like a Boss with Chris Voss")
- Labeling: soft observation of emotion ("It seems like...") — labeling a negative shrinks it, labeling a positive grows it. Mirroring: repeat their last ~3 words with downward inflection to make them self-reveal (Young and Profiting — "Learn How to NEGOTIATE Like a Boss with Chris Voss")
- Accusation audit + calibrated "what/how" questions + "no"-oriented questions ("Do you disagree?") give autonomy and surface real commitment (Young and Profiting — "The Art and Science Behind Negotiation with Chris Voss")
- "Tell me..." opener + Land the Plane: open them first, then go silent — most can't tolerate the silence and reveal more or accept. Mirror (internal prep) vs Window (across-table) questions (Young and Profiting — "How To Ask For A Raise... with Alexandra Carter")
- The 3 F's daily system: Follow Up (recent leads), Follow Through (do exactly what you said, when), Follow Back (past clients, dead deals, even the not-interested). "Balls Up" — keep many deals in the air so when one drops you have 16 others (Young and Profiting — "Real Estate Rockstar with @Ryan Serhant...")
- "5 new people a day" rule: meet 5, capture contact, feed them newsletters + follows + follow-up; compounds into the whole pipeline (Young and Profiting — "Real Estate Rockstar with @Ryan Serhant...")
- 10-20-30 rule: 10 slides, 20 minutes, 30-point font minimum. 30-second clarity test: in the first 30 seconds everyone should understand what you do (be the F-18 off the deck, not the A380 needing two miles of runway) (Young and Profiting — "Guy Kawasaki...")
- Three pillars of enchantment: likability + competence + trustworthiness — you need all three. "Democratize" positioning: name the gatekeeper your product removes (Mac democratized computing, Canva democratized design) (Young and Profiting — "Guy Kawasaki...")
- The 8-second rule: viewers decide within 8 seconds; thumbnail, title, topic are your first three hooks — open with a curiosity gap (just enough to spark, not satisfy). Three Rs of story: Repeatable, Relay emotion, Reframe beliefs (Young and Profiting — "Hook Your Audience in 8 SECONDS...")

### VOC language
- "Some people might not know what that means" / "real broad... everything" — buyer reaction to a vague title like "fractional CMO" or "multimedia designer" (The Futur — "Win More Clients With This Simple Pitch Hack")
- "It sucks to pitch work you really want, for budgets you can only dream of, and for four out of five to say 'no, not today, not you — someone else.'" — demoralized-agency dream-pain (The Futur — "Win More Clients With This Simple Pitch Hack")
- "I really don't want to spend more than $1,000." / "Can you do it cheaper?" / "Way too much." — verbatim low-ball / price pushback (The Futur — "How to Counter Low-ball Offers" / "How To Say Your Price")
- "I'm already sucked in the funnel, baby, and I didn't even know it." — buyer realizing they're being sold and can't get out (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script")
- Dream outcome: "I want them to look at me as a template for how to live their life." / "I want to look good in my pants." — deep emotional WHY vs surface vanity WHY (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script")
- Fear cluster: "fear of losing out... what if this doesn't work out, what if this is a waste of time or money, what if a client says no?" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- Sales = "ick": selling your own work feels "distasteful, self-centered"; the archetype is "used car salesman, timeshare, sleazy, Wolf of Wall Street" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- Dream outcome: "I'm ready for this struggle to be over... give me a soft landing place." Problems named: "an SEO problem, a conversion problem, a design problem, a branding problem, a messaging problem — I don't want to struggle anymore" (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition...")
- "What I don't tolerate is people who give me no evidence, no proof they can do what they say." (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition...")
- "Don't be Yoda. Don't be Miyagi. I don't need your Zen — just tell me what to do." (The Futur — "...Erwin McManus Teaches How To Identify Your Avatar")
- "I know what they're saying is right, but they're performing for me rather than communicating with me." — the "compelling but hollow" feeling toward inauthentic experts (The Futur — "...Erwin McManus...")
- "You're too expensive / you don't have enough experience / you don't know enough about [my niche]" — the three most common objections (The Futur — "How To Respond To The 3 Most Common Client Objections in Sales")
- "We had a designer before... every time we needed a small revision, they charged us extra. I don't want that kind of surprise again." / "It's not about the money, I just don't want any surprises." (The Futur — "The Real Job of a Sales Call")
- "Can I just get a Midjourney output for $10 versus paying you $10,000?" — the silent AI objection. "They're not going to tell you 'I didn't understand the proposal' — the unsaid is you losing the deal." (The Futur — "What Designers Do to Close $10K+ clients... | Ep. 346")
- "I want to be proud of how we're showing up in the marketplace / I want the experience to feel premium." — the real feeling-based desire under a logo request (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- The silent price objection: "I don't want you to think I'm cheap... that's so far out of what I can afford... I think I'm wasting your time." The polite brush-off that means ghost: "I have to go think about it" / "let me consider my options" (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- Do-nothing / hire-someone-else pain: "It takes too long to see results... you have no idea what they're doing... you just get a bill every month... if you don't like it you start over and burn another three months" (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- "I think it's important... not $1,000 important." — how prospects reveal a thing's true value to them (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- The fake objection: "I can't afford it" / "this is way more than I thought" / "it's just not worth it to me" — usually means the pain isn't big enough. "Just because I make a lot of money doesn't mean I'm going to pay $1,000 for a cup of water. It's relative to the pain." (The Futur — "Why People Buy... (w/ Jule Kim)")
- Why a buyer chose the pricier option: "It was a combination of vibe, a similar background, I just liked you... I went with you even though you cost more than twice as much." Identity objection: "It doesn't feel like me." (The Futur — "Why People Buy... (w/ Jule Kim)")
- "We overestimate the number of DIYers when in fact more of the audience are buyers" — buyers value their time; "sometimes the solution costs more than paying someone to do it right" (The Futur — "How to Sell Through Your Content in 2026")
- Demand pull that signals a product exists: "Can you please do a course on this? Can you write all your learnings in one place? I'll pay you for this." (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- Universal objection self-talk to mirror: "I've failed every time before" / "It's too hard for me to learn" / "This is too good to be true — maybe she can, but I can't" / "Am I too old? Is it too late?" (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- The dream-validation quote to engineer: "I've never heard anybody put it the way you do. I've paid $5,000, listened to 500 hours, and what you said in the first 15 minutes blows all the rest combined." (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Buyer/seller mindset: every seller "wants more money than their home is worth" and "doesn't care what the facts say"; buyers "want what they want for half the price, completely justified by their feelings." The fool's tell: "Well, it's up to you to convince me." (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- Hidden-cost objection reframed as desire: "You don't live in a million-dollar house, you live in a house that costs $4,500 a month... you live in the monthly payment." (Young and Profiting — "Real Estate Rockstar with @Ryan Serhant...")
- The generic, interchangeable pitch (what NOT to write): "We have patent-pending, curve-jumping, paradigm-shifting tech to dent the universe... while enabling our employees to self-actualize." (Young and Profiting — "Guy Kawasaki...")
- "People love to buy, but they hate being sold to." / "I don't have enough money / I don't know if it's worth it / I don't know if it'll work for me" — the three structural objections behind almost every no (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 1]" / "Why No One's Buying From You")
- Buyers fear "looking like an idiot" at work or fumbling procurement — they want guidance on who else to involve and what to expect (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary | Part 2")
- "Channel demand, don't create demand" — find a starving crowd with a mass problem rather than convince people they need you; prospects "talk themselves out of it" when given time (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Performance/risk-reversal offer: "I'll do the video for free. If we get the results you want, I'd like a percentage. No risk to you — I take all the risk." Then collapse to two clean options: pay $4K up front and keep all profit, OR free + 50% of new net revenue (The Futur — "How to Counter Low-ball Offers")
- Value-stacking the close: turn a $1,000 ask into ROI math out loud — "2–3 customers/day × $100 × 30 days = $7,500/month; does $1,000 seem appropriate?" Then "people spend money on what they value" (point to their BMW) (The Futur — "How to Counter Low-ball Offers")
- Discount only for pay-in-full: "$4,500 over 9 months, or $4,000 if you pay all up front — that's the only time you discount" (The Futur — "How to Sell Anything! $6,500 Sales Script")
- Paid Discovery Day: a $20K signed agreement before they even meet you ("if you give out free consulting, your opinion isn't very valuable"), plus a same-day refund guarantee; frame paid discovery as "dating before marriage" (The Futur — "Sales and Marketing Secrets... John Driscoll")
- $100M Offers principle: build the offer "so good a great salesperson isn't required"; adding guarantees + immediate bonuses changed close ratio overnight (The Futur — "Sales and Marketing Secrets... John Driscoll")
- Value-anchoring: "$10,000 is two and a half Louis Vuitton bags, or a fifth of a down payment on a 5-series" — "value is contextual; nothing is too expensive against nothing" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- Relative-scale pricing reveal: anchor every line item off the big number — "$60K on the logo but not $250K on the rollout? If you cheap out on production, it's lipstick on a pig" (The Futur — "How To Say Your Price")
- Testimonials as concrete receipts, not adjectives: "$60,000 annual contract," "landed a 5K client the week after," "closed a $200K/year job." Scarcity-as-proof: "limited to 30 people, already sold a third of London tickets" (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition...")
- Pricing IS positioning: with similar objects (water, wine, hotels) people assume the pricier thing is better; state your price plainly; for project fees say "projects start at [X]" to leave room to go up (The Futur — "The Real Job of a Sales Call")
- Set the benchmark with one yes: Chris decided strategy = "$10,000 a day," said it to everyone; the first person who agreed made it his real rate forever (The Futur — "The Real Job of a Sales Call")
- Pay-per-result offer: free upfront, vendor takes a % of measurable result (new customers above baseline), carries all risk; open at an "outrageous" anchor (50% in perpetuity) expecting to negotiate the % AND duration down. A guarantee is a priced add-on, not free — money-back makes the price go up exponentially (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- Match the commission % to client margins: only high-margin/high-LTV verticals (insurance, real estate, telecom, credit cards) can afford big CPA; protect any performance deal with an attorney-drafted contract + audit rights (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- Budget-elicitation question: "In what ballpark have you prepared in your mind to spend?" — mirror it back ("So you're prepared to spend $50–60k, is that right?") and set the rest relative to it (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- Charge value-based only when two conditions are met: the person values their time AND your work solves their problem; charge MORE for speed (the higher their net worth, the more their time is worth) (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- Stated retainer architecture: "My minimum engagement is $2,500/mo just to dedicate resources, up to $12,000/mo — let's find the number that feels comfortable." Raise prices on every NEW client (never re-price existing) to compound within a year (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Risk-mitigation close: 30-day trial at $X/mo with mutual benchmarks, bi-weekly report-and-redirect, then a one-page deal memo → invoice → start on payment. Phase big commitments (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Have a client filter: Can you deliver value? Would it bring joy? Do you like them? Is budget + timeline appropriate? Filters + specialization let the highest-paid charge most and keep a waitlist (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Give-it-all-away offer: "Make content so good, give it all away for free — no funnels, no email traps"; lead-magnet qualifier DM "Are you serious or just curious?" filters intent (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- Better design = higher win rate: when 3 proposals land at ~$10k and look the same, the more beautifully designed one signals "you'll care more," driving a 30–40% higher head-to-head win rate (The Futur — "What Designers Do to Close $10K+ clients... | Ep. 346")
- Reframe, don't discount: "It was $36k for a year — big commitment. It's $18k for 6 months." Same price, half the term, lands as "what a great price" (The Futur — "Generate Demand...")
- Strip bonuses, don't stack them: extra deliverables become distractions that make buyers want to pay less; remove until "they can't complain and they just buy" (The Futur — "Generate Demand...")
- The ultimate guarantee = buy-back: "We'll happily buy back whatever you bought" / pay them more than they paid to leave — churn and complaints collapse. Sell the feedback/result, give away the info (The Futur — "Generate Demand...")
- "Sell a taste before they buy": give one webinar/session free as a sample of being your customer, then offer the rest — "you've given them the product before they pay, no risk" (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- "Make the software free, sell the course": stop selling the tool; sell a $997–$2,000 course and include 12 months of top-tier software (a $3,600 value) as the bonus (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Best bonuses are "better than free" and un-pricable — exclusive software or something "not available anywhere at any price"; avoid books/ebooks (known $10–20 anchor) (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Second-chance scarcity close: run free content live, then "Remember I said I'd sell this? It's $37, but for the next 48 hours, $27" — people who saw it free, missed it, then got one more chance buy to avoid missing again (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Value-anchor risk reversal: "$2,000, but surveyed students rated it a $13,000 value. Full 30-day money-back guarantee, and I've never once had a refund." Webinar pricing sweet spot: $297–$2,000 closes one-to-many in ~90 min (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- 10x value rule: the offer should deliver ~10x the price so customers say "that was worth 10x" — that's what drives referrals; keep messaging on outcomes, not cost (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")
- Scarcity + urgency lines: "I can only take one client this month," "the contract I sent expires next week," "24-hour discount" (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")
- Risk-reversal/ROI guarantee: "Spend $5,000 with me; if you don't get $5,000 in ROI, I guarantee it — zero risk." Guarantees only work when results are strong and few claim them. Partnership framing over transactional: "I want a partnership, with my credibility on the line" (Young and Profiting — "Adam Schafer..." / "FREE WEBINAR...")
- Separate value from price: get a yes on the concept first ("In principle, does this feel good?"), reveal price after; if price is the objection, "I haven't sold you on the value properly." Price escalation: ladder up after each sale until you hit resistance (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 2]")
- Anchor high, quote low: float a higher range in discovery ("usually ~$100K/yr") so the real quote ($60K) reads as a discount. Pricing psychology: odd/precise ($4,997) signals analysis; round feels premium/un-discounted (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary | Part 2")
- Never give away value before commitment ("drug-dealer free sample" backfires): "as soon as you give value for free, you're by definition less valuable... people value things by what they paid." Never split the difference — loss feels 2x a gain (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- Price inside the search bracket: pricing $50k over "to leave room to negotiate" pushes you against bigger/better listings reduced into your bracket. Value-stack to justify: move-in-ready, furnished (quantify it), bigger lot, pool (Young and Profiting — "Real Estate Rockstar with @Ryan Serhant...")

### Objection handling
- Low-ball reframe — disqualify the budget, not yourself: "When someone says they don't have much money, my instinct is to say let's not do it. Where else could that $1,000 make a bigger impact?" Then refer them out (The Futur — "How to Counter Low-ball Offers")
- "You didn't have that $1,000 before they called — don't feel you HAVE to close it; that puts you in a disadvantaged position." Change the scope, not just the price: a 30-second video for $1,000 instead of a minute (The Futur — "How to Counter Low-ball Offers")
- Walk-away as genuine leverage: being ready to lose the deal is "attractive"; "not everybody who can afford you is your customer," and "if it's not a hell yes, it's a hell no" (The Futur — "Sales and Marketing Secrets... John Driscoll")
- The "what if" inversion: when a prospect fixates on downside, flip it — "What if this is a bargain? What if they've been dying to work with you? What if this is the beginning of something amazing?" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343" / "Why People Buy...")
- The "if nothing changes" close: "If nothing changes 3, 5, 10 years from now, do you see that version happier than today? If yes, don't change anything." Reframes inaction as the real risk (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- Who decides "fair": "You don't get to decide what's fair — the person you're selling to does." Plus "The price is the price. It's not my job to justify the value — if you can capture that value back, that's on you" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Selling... | Ep. 343")
- "Your problem is not special, but that doesn't mean YOU aren't special" — defuses the prospect who insists their nuance makes the standard solution not apply (The Futur — "Win More Clients With This Simple Pitch Hack")
- Beginner-overwhelm reframe as advantage: "If you've been doing sales completely wrong — good news, your room to grow is huge. Grab three pieces of low-hanging fruit and you improve ~50%" (The Futur — "Ditch the Competition...")
- Own it, then pivot: "You're right, we are too expensive / we don't have enough experience" — acknowledge first (otherwise you look slippery), validate, then point out why you're different (The Futur — "How To Respond To The 3 Most Common Client Objections in Sales")
- Raise the objection first to flip power: "I'm not sure a company of your size can afford us" — now THEY have to prove they can afford you. On a call: "I'm most likely going to be the highest bid. Is your decision based on how cheap it is, or on value?" (The Futur — "...3 Most Common Client Objections" / "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- "Only pay if it works" → ask "what business lets you eat the food, drive the car, then decide to pay later only if satisfied?" The premise fails the logic test (The Futur — "How to Negotiate When Clients Can't Afford Your Prices (Whiteboard)")
- Take-away / advisor close: "I'm not sure you need this — I don't think it's the best use of your time, money, or effort." Genuine, not a tactic; makes them say "wait, I will buy this from you" (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- Neediness repels: fix your finances first so you don't negotiate from a lack mindset — desperation skews your questions, tone, and footing (The Futur — "How To Charge For Design & Creative Work")
- "I don't know" builds trust (Paradox of Knowledge): "Great question, I've never been asked that — let me think and email you my answer." Admitting what you don't know makes them trust everything else (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- Price-pause reframe: don't assume a pause means "no" and discount yourself — name it neutrally: "It seems like you're feeling something about the price — what's happening?" (The Futur — "Never Get Ghosted Again... w/ Jule Kim (Part. 1)")
- Never justify your price: "justification concedes the higher ground." Just present it: "This is the price, I'm not really negotiable; if you don't want to work with me, I understand." A prospect who immediately challenges price is a red flag (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Make the unreasonable ask audible: get them to state it, play it back so they hear the absurdity ("red apples in the middle of the desert?"), then "How do you propose we do that and stay sustainable?" (The Futur — "60 Minute Sales Crash Course")
- Educate-then-release: before a price-shopper leaves, teach them the warning signs of someone who doesn't know what they're doing, so they self-disqualify cheaper bidders (The Futur — "Selling Without Being Salesy")
- Don't trust the stated objection — "I can't afford it" usually hides "the pain isn't big enough." Diagnose with questions before pitching: "you keep pushing because your ego's on the line. You're trying to convince instead of exploring" (The Futur — "Why People Buy... (w/ Jule Kim)")
- Reframe the "this isn't me" identity objection: "Fur coat, still you? Shave your head, still you? Then it's attachment to an idea of your identity used as leverage not to change. Do you want progress or comfort? Progress doesn't exist in the realm of comfort" (The Futur — "Why People Buy... (w/ Jule Kim)")
- Hit objections FIRST, not at the close: lay out every excuse/limiting belief up front, agree they're real, promise the answers by the end — disarmed before the pitch (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien... | Part 1")
- Don't over-scare: "if we just scare them into buying, we get their money once but create trauma." Sell hope alongside pain; "don't take their headache, turn it into a migraine, then sell them a Tylenol" (Young and Profiting — "Jason Fladlien..." / "4 Years...")
- Reframe selling as service: "If they saw themselves confidently moving forward with your solution, they'd be better off. This is not manipulation, this is service" (Young and Profiting — "4 Years of Sales Knowledge...")
- Loss-framing over gain-framing: people move on fear of loss, not opportunity. Flip "we'll get you 20% higher returns" to "do nothing and it costs you 20% every single day" (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- The "Why me?" qualifier: "You've got a lot of options, great competitors. Why me?" — surgical EQ strike that reveals favorite vs. fool. Then lay out the landscape and hand back control: "Here are the options, here are the consequences... How would you like to proceed?" (Young and Profiting — "Chris Voss & Steve Shull...")
- "What's the worst that can happen?" (kills approach anxiety): "What were they gonna do, say no? At least you know, and you move on." Disarming-honesty opener: "I have a quota to meet 5 new people a day, I've only met 4 — can you be my number 5?" (Young and Profiting — "Real Estate Rockstar with @Ryan Serhant...")
- Disqualify ruthlessly: politely push away no-budget/no-timeline/non-decision-makers ("let's reconnect in 6 months") — prospects respect it and self-qualify. Help them buy better, not easier: "let's bring the CEO/CMO next time" reframes a complex process as support (Young and Profiting — "Scott D. Clary | Part 2")
- Turn "no" into "yes" with "What are your concerns?" — let them diagnose the real objection. Kill reactance by reframing your role: "My job isn't to convince you — it's to help you decide if this is right for you" (Young and Profiting — "How To Ask For A Raise..." / "Why No One's Buying From You")
- "No"-oriented re-engagement for ghosters: "Are you no longer interested in X?" / "Did you decide to walk away from X?" plus a soft, "busy"-implies-other-options follow-up restarts dead threads (Young and Profiting — "FREE WEBINAR: Crush Your Sales Goals 2024")
- Pre-empt objections, don't rebut them: bake the doubt into the promise — "even if you're new to funnels or don't have a big following" clears it before it forms. Sell the outcome, not the effort (Young and Profiting — "Why No One's Buying From You")
- Emotion gates logic: the lizard brain must register a threat or opportunity before logic engages; the four wins that fire it are save time, save money, make money, and look good (ego is strongest). Don't quote on a maybe — loop back and find where you dropped the ball (Young and Profiting — "The Laws of Selling with Richard Moore [Part 2]")

- "You are not selling a commodity. You just lack imagination." (title-as-hook) (The Futur — "You Are Not Selling A Commodity")
- Be specific over clever: "an AI copywriter that writes your blog posts" beats "a fusion of AI and human design" (The Futur — "Write Better Copy For Conversions w/ Neville Medhora")

### Frameworks / formulas
- 3-step close: (1) find clients / build a lead pool, (2) build trust + diagnose their problem, (3) ask for the money — the engine behind $10M+ in closes (Alex Berman — "How have we crossed over 10 Million in Closes")
- 4-step prospect-list build: pick exactly who you sell to → find a lead pool (Google "largest X in the world") → find the named contact on LinkedIn → guess the email with Hunter/Voila Norbert (Alex Berman — "Q&A Cold Email 2019")
- Cold-email baseline targets: 80% open, 20% reply, 4-6% meeting-book rate; test in batches of ~40-200, change subject every 10, rewrite body on unsubscribes (Alex Berman — "Q&A Cold Email 2019" / "Cold Email Teardown — Dentists")
- Scale safely: 10-15 G Suite inboxes, ≤50 sends/day/inbox; if open rate drops fix subject, bounces fix lead quality, replies drop fix script, bookings drop fix the appointment-setting step (Alex Berman — "Cold Email Teardown — Dentists")
- Niche down hard: not "SaaS" or "all B2B" but "financial-services SaaS built on WordPress" — specificity is the single biggest reply-rate lever alongside data accuracy (Alex Berman — "Cold Email in an Oversaturated Market 2022")
- Discovery call = diagnose like a doctor: intro → short value prop → discovery questions → confirm value prop → close for the next meeting; always book the next call before hanging up (Alex Berman — "How to Run a Sales Discovery Call 2021")
- Personalized riffed video > scripted generic: screen-share their site/channel, show the specific fix, "show don't tell" (Alex Berman — "Cold Email Custom Video Pitches")
- Know-Like-Trust: people hire who they know, like, trust — even someone less talented; "knowing" = marketing (The Futur — "Basic Steps On How To Get More Sales")
- "Amateurs give advice; experts diagnose." Stay in the diagnostic phase as long as possible and get paid to think, not just make (The Futur — "Basic Steps On How To Get More Sales")
- Win Without Pitching: get verbal commitment on the call ("do with words what we used to do with paper"), then send a one-page deal memo to sign — never pitch a solution (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique – Clubhouse Roleplay")
- Embrace-and-Pivot: client comes for one service, thank them, then pivot up — "I've added a new thing that's really helped my clients grow... are you curious?" (The Futur — "How To Go From Design To Selling Strategy")
- Pre-call prep = 3 lists: (1) who the customer is + their pain, (2) every likely objection (circle top 3, prep answers), (3) two columns — what they need vs what you need from the call (The Futur — "Do This Before Your Next Client Call")
- Call sequence = Money → Deadline → Scope (no point on scope if money/timeline don't work) (The Futur — "Do This Before Your Next Client Call")
- SALES = Serve, Ask, Listen, Empathize, Summarize — the non-salesy close framework (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Being Salesy")
- 3 qualifiers before pursuing any prospect: do I like them? is there work I can do? can they afford me? (The Futur — "How To Ask for the Sale - Part 1")
- Question hierarchy: "What" opens neutrally; "How" rushes to tactics; "Why" sounds accusatory — lead with What (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Being Salesy")
- 3 tones of voice (Voss): Assertive (usually backfires), Accommodator (smiling — best for bad news), Analyst / late-night-FM-DJ (low, downward inflection — draws a firm line calmly; drop your chin to hit it) (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator" / "5 Sales Skills")
- Copy → Combine → Transform; and Shu-Ha-Ri (preserve the master's method, then break it, then forge your own) — master before you innovate (The Futur — "Why Copying Works")
- Reframing = change the question, not the answer: "make the elevator faster" → "reduce the frustration of waiting" unlocks cheap solutions (mirrors, music) (The Futur — "Why Copying Works")
- 3 positioning steps: choose a focus (discipline × market) → articulate it as a claim of expertise → build skills to back it; make the claim before you're ready so it forces you to build (The Futur — "Focus To Build Expertise Rapidly")
- Buying-cycle weighting: early buyers overweight the upside (inspire them); late buyers overweight the cost of failure (reassure them) — shift from inspiring to reassuring at the close (The Futur — "Focus To Build Expertise Rapidly")
- 6 steps to a sale: prospect → qualify → approach → presentation → objection → close (qualify on budget, authority, desire) (The Futur — "One Thing You Should Never Do In Sales")
- "Don't sell past the close": the moment they form intent to buy, STOP — nothing to gain, everything to lose (The Futur — "One Thing You Should Never Do In Sales")
- Conditional "if-then" close: "if" is safe and hypothetical — walk them from hypothetical to real with tiny yes-decisions (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Being Salesy")
- Context-first pitching: "Before the details, let me give you a frame of reference so you know how to evaluate this" (The Futur — "Pitch This!")
- 5 Ingredients technique: break any work into ~5 observable (objective, not interpretive) components so you can recreate without copying (The Futur — "How To Copy Without Stealing")
- Charge for Discovery: "if you can solve a client's problem through talking, you should charge for it" — call it strategy / Discovery / brand audit; start with a nominal fee to prove it's worth money (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call — Melinda Livsey Ep7")

### VOC language
- "I really have a problem acquiring the right type of clients... the inquiries we get just aren't qualified leads" (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique – Clubhouse Roleplay")
- "How short can I be? Is it going to bring me the results that I want?" (prospect's core risk objection) (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique")
- "When you mentioned the money-back guarantee and that someone's actually working until I get the result, it's really reassuring" (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique")
- The buyer's silent test before hiring: "Do you recognize me? Do you understand my problem, my wants, my fears and hopes — before you start selling me?" (The Futur — "5 Sales Skills To Close More Sales")
- "We all have this allergic reaction when someone reaches out their hand and tries to sell to us immediately" (The Futur — "5 Sales Skills")
- The commodity complaint (verbatim): "Chris, I can't charge more — there's too much competition; if I don't charge less, someone down the street will" (The Futur — "You Are Not Selling A Commodity")
- Developing-market pain: "Dude, no one here wants to pay for what it's worth" (The Futur — "You Are Not Selling A Commodity")
- Real client buying reason: "We really want to go with you because we felt validated — you're so enthusiastic about our project" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call — Melinda Livsey")
- Live pricing objections: "What do I get for that $10,000?" / "Why is redesigning our logo so expensive?" / "That sounds like a lot" / "I'm hoping we can afford you" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call")
- Employee-to-founder trigger: "I'm just upselling clients and making my CEO richer while my salary stays the same" (The Futur — "Pitching Your Way to Success")
- Small-business pain that founds categories: people with "zero money, zero budget, and zero clue" who "don't have the budget to spend three grand a month telling their stories" (The Futur — "Pitching Your Way to Success")
- Testimonial gold: "I've run an ad agency for 25 years and this is the first time in my career I've ever felt like the expert" (The Futur — "Focus To Build Expertise Rapidly")
- The "easy for you to say" objection: "Easy for you to say because you're X, Y, Z — easy for Chris Voss to say 'we don't do work for hire'" (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")

### Offers / pricing / guarantees
- Risk-reversal stack: small money up front + try it a couple months + cancel option + high-% money-back guarantee — "if we don't hit these numbers, you don't pay us a thing" (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique")
- Performance pricing tied to the client's own stated number: "30% of the gross... and I don't stop working until you get your results" (The Futur — "Easy Sales Technique")
- Price-anchor move: give a free strategic taste, then "the next meeting's on you — I typically charge $10k for this" (The Futur — "How To Go From Design To Selling Strategy")
- Price the customer's PROFIT, not cost+margin — "every dollar they spend, they get back 10x"; and say "money," never "budget" (budget sounds cheap) — "How much money have you set aside for this?" (The Futur — "How To Talk About Money – Dan Mall")
- Sliding scale by client risk: same website is $40k or $300k depending on their exposure (stock price, investors), not your hours; add a rush charge and a "pain-in-the-butt charge" (nitpicky = you under-charged) (The Futur — "How To Talk About Money – Dan Mall")
- Pricing script (steal verbatim): "I don't have a rate. I'll spend as much time as I can understanding what you need, then come up with options that feel like a steal for you and are lucrative for me — I want us both to profit" (The Futur — "How To Talk About Money – Dan Mall")
- Conditional-close worked script: "If a website lifted conversion 2%→4%, adding $400k profit this year, that's a home run?" → "Yes" → "If we send a $65,000 proposal by EOD, you're ready to move next week — correct?" (The Futur — "How to Sell Without Being Salesy")
- Budget-qualifying questions: "Do you mind sharing your budget?" / "What have you spent on something like this before?" / "Give me an average, I won't hold you to it" / "Closer to $50k or $500k?" (The Futur — "How To Ask for the Sale - Part 1")
- Pre-qualify on price BEFORE writing any proposal — "If we come back with a bid in this range, are you okay with that?" asked so they can say no without losing face; "you get paid exactly zero dollars to build proposals" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call")
- Tiered anchoring stated up front: branding $8-10k, packaging starts $5k, websites start $15k — "starting at... depends on complexity" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call")
- Value-pricing principle: no such thing as a commodity, only a lack of imagination — a $1.69 head of lettuce becomes a $4 bagged salad, then an $11.99 branded Caesar kit (The Futur — "You Are Not Selling A Commodity")
- Hold the IP line: "We don't do work for hire" — that gives away the intellectual property, which is what you're actually selling (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")
- Soft CTA > hard CTA on content: "buy my course" negates the goodwill; prefer subscribe/listen — but "zero call to action, you'll probably make no money" (The Futur — "How to Script a YouTube Video")
- Self-select on the page: state who you serve and what it costs so poor-fit leads filter themselves ("we only serve vegan, so no one complains there's no beef") (The Futur — "Do This Before Your Next Client Call")
- 160 minutes with pen and paper beats spending $160,000 on an agency to "come up with a concept"; golden rule: don't spend on product development before you have customers (Alex Berman — "Sales System Only Works If You're Rich")
- In real estate, data quality is the offer's foundation: skip-tracing (25¢-$2/record) + signals (assessed << market value, absentee owner, tax delinquency) find the motivated seller; direct mail = 1-3% reply on a good day (Alex Berman — "Property Owner Lookup")

### Objection handling
- "Why haven't you done that before?" — turn the "I'll just hire someone in-house" objection back into a question that surfaces why they haven't (The Futur — "8 Client Objection Responses in 8 Minutes")
- Doctor reframe for paid discovery ("why am I paying you to learn my business?"): "When the doctor runs a battery of tests, do you want them done for free? You don't understand the problem or how to solve it — yet you want to tell me how to solve it for you" (The Futur — "8 Client Objection Responses")
- "Send me a packet and I'll get back to you" stall: "Before I send a document you most likely won't read — are we in agreement on price, scope, and deliverables?" (The Futur — "8 Client Objection Responses")
- "All I need is a logo": "When I show you just a logo, will you know by looking at it whether it'll work for you or not?" — exposes the missing strategy (The Futur — "8 Client Objection Responses")
- "No proof / no case studies" objection: "Did the plan I laid out make sense to you? You could take that plan to someone else if you'd like" — confidence over neediness (The Futur — "8 Client Objection Responses")
- "You're too expensive" → shift cost to value: "If this delivered on everything, what would the impact on your business be — the cost of building it, or much larger?" Reframe price as ROI / investment (The Futur — "How to respond to the 3 most common Client Objections")
- The rock-paper-scissors trap: a mid-size firm loses on price to the small shop AND on experience to the giant — so don't compete on either; reducing scope to cut price just makes the small player win (The Futur — "How to respond to the 3 most common Client Objections")
- "Just do it cheaply / it's not that serious" objection: mirror the contradiction back ("you don't want it cheap, you care about quality, you want it shared — so it does matter"), label the emotion ("am I annoying you right now?"), and surface the real driver before quoting (The Futur — "How To Respond When The Client Just Wants It Done Cheaply")
- Surface unspoken objections: state every objection they're thinking but haven't voiced ("you're concerned there are two teams not one, and I'll tell you why that's a benefit") — squash them before they're mouthed (The Futur — "Surfacing Unspoken Objections")
- Demonstrate expertise by asking great questions, not claiming it: "that's how you know somebody knows something" (The Futur — "Surfacing Unspoken Objections")
- "I need a moment to think about that — great question": an intelligent person doesn't answer fast; follow-up questions often make the prospect answer their own poorly-formed question (The Futur — "Surfacing Unspoken Objections")
- Never chase "yes" (commitment vs confirmation vs counterfeit) — a tactical "no" is safer than five yeses; "have you got a few minutes?" makes everyone defensive (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")
- Test if you're really in the running with a "what" question, not "are we your top choice?": "On a scale of 1-10, what's our chance here?" — the hesitation matters more than the number (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")
- Move a firm position without triggering reciprocity: state the boundary as fact, then go silent — "if I ask them to remove the clause, I owe"; silence makes them volunteer the concession (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")
- Raised objections are buying signals — "otherwise they'd politely nod and move on; they just need more information" — take notes to show you're listening (The Futur — "One Thing You Should Never Do In Sales")
- Last impression = lasting impression: exit a stalled deal so you're who they call later — "I'd be happy to do business when you're ready; I can accept you're not ready right now" (The Futur — "FBI Negotiator")
- The filter as desire-builder: telling a prospect "you might be a poor fit for us" and creating real/artificial barriers makes them want you more — "this person doesn't even need my business, yet still wants to work with me" (The Futur — "5 Sales Skills")
- Disarm "is this too much money?" by making it safe to walk: ask the price-range question "so they can say no without losing face" — like browsing a luxury store, nobody blurts "I can't afford this" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call")
- "Can the client afford us?" reframed as scarcity: "If we're not in the same ballpark I can't work with you — not that I don't want to, but I have limited time and can only take so many clients" (The Futur — "First Client Meeting Sales Call")
- Tone as a trust signal: talking fast spikes the prospect's anxiety ("is he desperate?") and kills trust; slow, low, deliberate delivery calms even an angry buyer (The Futur — "5 Sales Skills")
- "You're probably right, but let's make sure" — agree-but-verify reframe for a client-prescribed bad solution (The Futur — "Blair Enns Interview")
- Neediness repels: "nothing is more repelling than someone desperate"; confidence comes from reviewing your own portfolio/testimonials before the call — never enter needy (The Futur — "How to Get Clients" / "Do This Before Your Next Client Call")

- Open by listing the prospect's painful status quo, then: "what would be different in your business if you had a predictable way to generate leads and more opportunity than you knew what to do with?" (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
### Frameworks / formulas
- The "irresistible offer" lives at the TOP of the funnel, before anyone does business with you — its only job is to get ideal prospects to raise their hand and say "this is awesome, I want it" (not to make your core offer better) (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- 3 big ideas behind it: (1) remove the risk/friction, (2) give before you ask (social-exchange theory — giving makes them like you, trust you, want to reciprocate), (3) stretch the gap between where they are and where they want to be (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- Every prospect action = a risk/reward balance; the best customer journeys make each step easy, low-risk, with a clear benefit. "The more reward you front-load, the more people want it." (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- 4 risks to neutralize: time, money, energy, and STATUS ("how will I look to others if this messes up — people want to avoid looking like an idiot"); design the offer to amplify their social status (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- An irresistible offer should do 3 things: (1) give clarity on their real problem / what's keeping them stuck, (2) show the cost of NOT fixing it (money left on the table), (3) get them excited about "Island B" / what's possible (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- "People don't pay big money to solve small problems" (Daniel Priestley) — stretch the gap = show them the true size of the problem, and that the problem they came with often isn't the one they need to fix (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
### VOC language

- Why prospects ignore "jump on a call" offers: "it's intrusive, annoying — I'm worried about getting hard sold and wasting my time" (the risk outweighs the reward) (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- Prospect's #1 buying fear (verbatim): "I'm going to give time, money and energy and not get back what I want and need from this thing" (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
### Objection handling
- Eliminate sales fear by giving value up front: demonstrate you can solve the problem before asking — "people buy from people they like and trust"; the scales flip from resistance to "I want this, how do I work with you?" (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")
- Reframe the hard sell as service via "give before you ask" — approach from a place of giving so it never feels salesy, then hand-pick who you advance (The Futur — "A New Approach To Selling — Matt Essam")

- Plant doubt about the competitor by stretching their pitch to its extreme, then jab: voice what the client secretly worries the rival can't handle, agree with it out loud, then show why you cover it (The Futur — "Use This Sales Technique The Next Time You Pitch")

- Stalled deal where your contact isn't the decision-maker: ping the boss directly — "Mark said he'd sign 3 days ago and hasn't, any update?" — the CEO forwards it back and it closes (Alex Berman — "3 Ways to Close Deals Faster")
- Don't lie / don't stretch claims — "Hong Kong's largest insurance firm" is instantly Google-checkable and kills trust; soften unverified results to future tense ("will more effectively attract...") (Alex Berman — "3 Important Questions")

### Objection handling
- Take objections off the table first: "Before we go further — I'm probably too expensive, probably don't have the exact experience you want, and I can't guarantee results. - Conditional-question reframe (turns their trait against them): "IF technical specs matter most to you, then you should hire someone else — but if you want [the real outcome]..." forces them to rank what they actually value (The Futur — "Be The First To Raise Client Objections")
- Price-anchor a 2x quote before revealing it: "I'd prefer to be the LAST person you talk to, because I'll be about twice what others quote — but ask everyone else this one question first: show me examples that prove you can actually do this" (The Futur — "The Sales Strategy to Beat the Competition")
- Price-check on call one to disqualify fast: "that marketing review typically runs $20-30k" then go silent — "that's crazy money" = unqualified, saves the whole funnel (Alex Berman — "5 Tips to Close more B2B Sales")
- Mirroring reversal: repeat their exact word + tone, then pivot — "Look, I know you have no interest in this tool right now... but are you interested in improving your conversion rate?" (Alex Berman — "Master These 26 Sales Tricks")
- Breakup email to force a yes/no: "I was really looking forward to talking... I haven't heard back and I'm sure you're busy, so this'll be my last email — if you change your mind, always happy to chat" (Alex Berman — "Master These 26 Sales Tricks")
- Contrast principle: present the painful alternative first — "you could hire a team of US reps 24/7 for $3-4M a year, OR use our tool for $99/mo" (Alex Berman — "Master These 26 Sales Tricks")

- Irresistible-offer mechanics (infomercial): odd price ($1,199.99 not $1,000), stack bonuses ("second knife FREE + six free steak knives"), "add more items and DROP the price," break into multipay, then build back-end continuity. People now EXPECT something extra. (Kevin Harrington via Lewis Howes)
- Clay-personalized outbound: dynamic prefix "saw you specialize in {AI-pulled company specialty}..." concatenated onto the case-study line for mass-but-personalized cold email at volume. (Alex Berman — "How We Send 144,000 Cold Emails per Month With Clay")

### Objection handling
- No-oriented questions (swipe verbatim): "Is now a bad time to talk?" (not "got a few minutes?"), "Do you disagree?" (not "do you agree?"), "Is this a ridiculous idea?" / "Are you against...?" A "no" makes people feel safe and in control, then they hand you the real problems to solve — "no, but I can't agree until you fix X" = a path forward. Practice low-stakes to build the reflex. (Chris Voss via Young and Profiting — "Get people to say NO")
- 3 reasons clients ask for discounts + counters: (1) too much RISK → don't discount, remove risk with a hyper-custom pitch that proves you understand them; (2) résumé play (enterprise negotiator must "show they negotiated") → give a free add-on (e.g. unlimited follow-ups), never a price cut; (3) genuinely no money → restate your pricing and let them walk ("defend your rates to the grave") — they self-select out and you dodge the future refund. (Alex Berman — "Negotiation Tactics: 3 Reasons Clients Ask for Discounts")
- Commission-only / free-trial pushback = a risk objection in disguise; answer by explaining WHY commission-only fails and demonstrating value, and the buyer "finds the marketing budget." (Alex Berman — "Negotiation Tactics")
- Surface obstacles early (minute 5, not 44): "If we get to the end and it's a fit, what would need to be true for you to move forward this week?" Obstacles (budget timing, needs a partner, legal) you can solve; objections you must diagnose. Qualify before booking: "current monthly revenue?" + "who else besides you decides on vendor spend?" (Alex Berman — "5 beliefs")
- Risk-reversal via third-party proof: put a named testimonial directly BELOW the opt-in button — at the moment of action buyers hesitate ("is this the right move?") and a well-known quote "seals the deal." (Derek Halpern via Lewis Howes — "How To Increase Sales")

- WIIFM reframe that reverses a cost objection: recast an under-used asset as new value — "every employee's LinkedIn profile is a mini-website that brands your company and drives traffic back" (Brandon Bornancin — "Stan Robinson Jr Are You Tuned Into Your Buyer's Station")
- ROI reframe on price: "the subscription fee will seem like nothing when you're booking two extra demos a week" (Brandon Bornancin — "We DOUBLED our Sales to make over $1M with Seamless! Wade Brogdon, LogMeIn")
- Beat internal bureaucracy: "Don't listen to your director — just try it. Do a trial, put it through petty cash... selling internally is harder than selling externally" (Brandon Bornancin — "We DOUBLED our Sales to make over $1M with Seamless! Wade Brogdon, LogMeIn")
- "Channel doesn't work" objection: anyone who says email/calling/social/video 'doesn't work' loses intelligence points — every channel works, run omni-channel (Brandon Bornancin — "Make Time for Your Prospects!")
- Hunter's posture on the "maybe": "We want a yes or no... we're actually looking for the no, because it gets us to the essence faster" (Brandon Bornancin — "Marylou Tyler Focus On Habit")
- Pre-empt distrust by leading with weakness: "here's some things we suck at right now... you're gonna find out anyway, so let's lead with it" — buyers become "magnets to that dial" (Brandon Bornancin — "Todd Caponi Why Imperfection Sells")

- **Transparent pricing as differentiator**: "No secret pricing you have to get on 19 calls for — we present the pricing right away at the end" (Brandon Bornancin — "Try This 3 Step Sales Demo Strategy").
- **Quantified outcome stack for the close**: "book 3–5x more appointments, double your sales, increase appointments 300–500%" — lead the close with dream-outcome numbers (Brandon Bornancin — "Try This 3 Step Sales Demo Strategy").
- **Achievement-recognition loop**: customer hits six/seven figures with the product → applies → you ship a custom $1,000 "President's Club" award (14k six-fig + 4.5k seven-fig winners) — turns buyers into proof + referrers (Brandon Bornancin — "The Sales List Is KING").
- **Price anchoring by category**: sub-$100/mo SaaS is a totally different sell than $100k–$20M enterprise deals — build a repeatable pitch for the price point, don't reuse enterprise choreography on low-ticket (Brandon Bornancin — "Try This 3 Step Sales Demo Strategy").

### Objection handling
- **Annual-contract reframe (full script)**: "Yes, contracts are annual by default. We found customers who commit to a full year are more successful than anyone else over the long term — and since your long-term success is our mission, we have to encourage the practices that support it. Sign here and here." (Brandon Bornancin — "Why Prospects Should Commit To Annual Deals").
- **Never cut price OR length**: "Reducing price or contract length doesn't increase value to the customer — the only way to increase value is to keep investing in the product, and that requires annual commitments" (Brandon Bornancin — "Why Prospects Should Commit To Annual Deals").
- **Assume-responsibility flip**: the moment you hear yourself make an excuse ("price too high"), reframe to "how can I create the value to command this price?" (Brandon Bornancin — "Sales Quota Killers").
- **Block, don't overcome**: pre-frame likely objections so they never surface, instead of rebutting them after the fact (Victor Antonio — "Don't Overcome Objections, Block Them").
- **Contrarian CAC reframe for value-selling**: gurus cap acquisition cost at 20–30% of contract value; the real question is "how much would you spend to make $36k?" — sell the maximum-upside math, not the minimum-cost math (Brandon Bornancin — "How Much Does it Cost to NOT Acquire a Customer?").
